\documentclass[sigconf]{acmart}

\setcopyright{none}
\settopmatter{printacmref=false}
\renewcommand\footnotetextcopyrightpermission[1]{}
\pagestyle{plain}

\usepackage{booktabs}
\usepackage{array}
\usepackage{xspace}
\usepackage{url}
\usepackage{graphicx}

\newcommand{\toolname}{\textsc{AgentPProf}\xspace}
\newcommand{\operation}{\texttt{operation}\xspace}
\newcommand{\opstack}{\texttt{operation stack}\xspace}

\begin{document}

\title{AgentPProf: Semantic Profiling for AI Agent Traces}

\begin{abstract}
% Beat 1: Context
AI agents produce complex execution traces spanning prompts, LLM calls,
tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects. As deployments grow
to hundreds of sessions, both human operators and automated analysis
pipelines need aggregate views---not just per-execution debugging.

% Beat 2: Problem
Existing observability tools organize events into fixed session/span
hierarchies suited for single-run debugging but unable to fold events
across sessions by semantic work category. CPU flame graphs solve the
equivalent aggregation problem for programs, but they rely on
deterministic function names, but agent prompts are natural language and
cannot be folded directly.

% Beat 3: This paper
We show that agent profiling reduces to two abstractions once intent
recognition restores the deterministic-label precondition. An
\emph{operation} is a uniform weighted record for any agent activity; an
\emph{operation stack} is a field projection chosen at query time.
Sessions and spans become optional fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
\toolname implements this model with pluggable intent-recognition
backends (regex rules, local LLM tagging, unsupervised clustering) and
produces flame graphs, pprof profiles, and structured JSON consumable by
both developers and analysis agents.

% Beat 4: Results
On 325 real agent sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of
system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public datasets
(34{,}539 operations), operation-stack profiling reduces inspection work
by 90\% versus flat summaries and fragmentation by 45\% versus
fixed-session drilldown. Leave-dataset-out mapping achieves V-measure
above 0.7 on 7/9 held-out datasets.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

%% ===================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

AI agent systems produce execution traces that interleave prompts, LLM
calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, process events, and benchmark
labels. As agent deployments scale to hundreds of sessions and tens of
thousands of calls, both developers and automated analysis agents need
to answer aggregate questions: which categories of work consume the most
tokens, where do repeated failures concentrate, and how does cost
distribute across semantic task families? Existing observability
tools---LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel}---organize
events into per-execution timelines and span trees, enabling
single-run debugging. But no existing tool provides an aggregate view
that folds heterogeneous events across sessions into a cost or frequency
distribution grouped by semantic work category.

CPU profilers solved the equivalent problem for programs: flame
graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} fold millions of function-call samples into
a single chart where width represents cost. The key enabler is
\emph{deterministic} function names that merge identical call stacks.
Agent traces break this assumption---prompts are natural language, and
two prompts expressing the same intent share no characters. We develop
this gap and the design requirements it implies in
\S\ref{sec:background}.

The central insight is that agent observability requires
\emph{profiling}: aggregate, cross-session cost attribution grouped by
user intent---which we call \emph{semantic} to distinguish from
execution-structural groupings like sessions or spans. The obstacle to
applying classical profiler techniques is the nondeterminism of
natural-language identifiers. This paper presents \toolname, a profiler
that restores aggregate flame-graph analysis for agent traces. The
profiler is built on two abstractions: an \emph{operation} (a uniform
weighted record for any agent activity) and an \emph{operation stack}
(a field projection chosen at query time). Sessions, spans, and trace
identifiers are operation fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
\emph{Intent recognition}---mapping free-form prompts to stable labels
through pluggable backends (regex rules, local LLM tagging, or
unsupervised clustering)---restores the deterministic-label precondition
that flame-graph folding requires.

Some existing tools take steps toward semantic grouping: Datadog LLM
Observability clusters user messages by
topic,\footnote{\url{https://docs.datadoghq.com/llm_observability/}}
and Laminar extracts structured signals from
traces.\footnote{\url{https://docs.lmnr.ai/signals/introduction}} These tools characterize \emph{input
distributions} (``30\% of users ask code questions'') but not
\emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks consume 40\% of the
token budget''). \toolname produces the latter through folded-stack
aggregation where width represents cost.

This paper makes three contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Insight: agent profiling reduces to two abstractions.}
  We show that the aggregation gap in agent observability---fixed
  session/span hierarchies cannot fold by semantic category---is closed
  by combining uniform operation records with query-time stack
  projections, once intent recognition restores deterministic labels
  (\S\ref{sec:background}--\S\ref{sec:design}).
\item \textbf{System: \toolname.}
  We implement this model as a Rust CLI with pluggable intent
  recognition, four built-in views, and output formats (pprof, SVG,
  JSON) consumable by both developers and automated analysis agents
  (\S\ref{sec:impl}).
\item \textbf{Evaluation.}
  We show that semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight
  that unsemantic views merge (RQ1), that operation-stack profiling
  localizes hidden labeled problems with 90\% less work than flat
  summaries (RQ2), and that mapping-derived labels agree with
  ground-truth annotations on 7/9 public datasets (RQ3)
  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
\end{enumerate}

%% ===================================================================
\section{Background and Motivation}
\label{sec:background}

\subsection{How Existing Agent Trace Models Work}

Current agent observability tools organize traces around fixed
hierarchies. OpenTelemetry represents an execution as a \emph{trace}
containing a tree of \emph{spans}, each with a name, duration, and
key-value attributes. LangSmith and Langfuse group spans into
\emph{sessions} and display them as timelines or waterfall charts.
Phoenix and OpenInference add GenAI-specific span types for LLM calls,
tool invocations, retrieval steps, and agent reasoning.

These models share a structural property: the session or span tree is the
skeleton of the data. Every event belongs to exactly one span, and spans
nest in a fixed parent-child hierarchy determined at execution time.
This design is effective for debugging: a developer can locate a failing
span, inspect its attributes, and trace its parent chain to understand
the execution context.

\subsection{Why Fixed Hierarchies Cannot Profile}

Profiling requires a fundamentally different operation: \emph{folding}
events across executions by semantic category so that width represents
aggregate cost. Fixed session/span hierarchies obstruct this in three
ways.

\paragraph{Sessions are boundaries, not categories.}
A session groups events by execution, not by intent. A single session
may contain review, debugging, and refactoring phases. Splitting by
session assigns all of them to the same bucket. Conversely, two sessions
performing the same task produce two separate buckets that cannot be
merged without external logic.

\paragraph{Span names are not semantic labels.}
Span names describe mechanisms (\texttt{LLMCall}, \texttt{ToolInvoke},
\texttt{ChatCompletion}), not user intent (\texttt{review},
\texttt{debug}, \texttt{test}). Grouping by span name tells you how many
LLM calls occurred, not which categories of work consumed the budget.

\paragraph{Concrete example.}
In a real development project, the system effect
\texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok} appears 2{,}903 times
across 325 sessions. A flat process summary shows a single counter; no
existing trace tool can disaggregate these executions by the semantic
intent that triggered them. We quantify this disaggregation in
RQ1~(\S\ref{sec:eval}).

\subsection{Why CPU Profiling Does Not Directly Apply}

CPU profilers solve the equivalent aggregation problem for programs.
A flame graph~\cite{flamegraphs} represents a profile as a set of
weighted \emph{samples}, each attached to a \emph{call stack} (an
ordered list of function frames). Identical stacks merge, and width
represents aggregate cost. The key enabler is that function names are
\emph{deterministic}: the same code path always produces the same
frames.

Agent traces break this precondition. As noted in \S\ref{sec:intro}, prompts are
natural language and lack deterministic identifiers. Tool calls, GUI
actions, and process events are named heterogeneously across agent
families. Raw event names cannot serve as flame-graph frames.

These observations yield three design requirements:

\begin{description}
\item[R1: Uniform record type.]
  Agent traces mix prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions,
  process events, and benchmark labels. The profiler needs a single
  record type that can represent all of them without type-specific
  objects.
\item[R2: Query-time aggregation.]
  The same data must support multiple aggregation shapes---by task,
  phase, action, session, or dataset---without rebuilding the trace.
  Sessions and spans must be fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
\item[R3: Deterministic labels for folding.]
  Free-form prompts must be mapped to short, stable, repeatable labels
  before folding. This \emph{intent recognition} step has no analogue in
  CPU profiling, where function names are already deterministic.
\end{description}

\section{Design}
\label{sec:design}

The three requirements from \S\ref{sec:background} drive the design.
We introduce two abstractions---operations (\S\ref{sec:ops}) and
operation stacks (\S\ref{sec:stacks})---that satisfy R1 and R2, and a
pluggable intent-recognition mechanism (\S\ref{sec:intent}) that
satisfies R3.

\subsection{Operations (R1: Uniform Record Type)}
\label{sec:ops}

A profiler should not distinguish between prompts, tool calls, and
process events at the object-model level. \toolname uses a single
abstraction: an \operation is a weighted record with string fields and
additive measures.

Each operation carries string fields (\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent},
\texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag}, \texttt{kind}, \texttt{model},
\texttt{path}, \texttt{domain}, \texttt{status}, \ldots) and additive
measures (token count, duration, occurrence count). A prompt, an LLM
call, a tool invocation, a file read, a GUI click, and a process event
are all operation records that differ only in which fields are populated.
This satisfies R1: the profiler does not need to distinguish event types
at the object-model level.

\subsection{Operation Stacks (R2: Query-Time Aggregation)}
\label{sec:stacks}

An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time. Folding
operations by that list produces the standard folded-stack
representation:

\begin{small}
\begin{verbatim}
CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
\end{verbatim}
\end{small}

\noindent Unlike CPU profiling, where the call stack is determined by
execution, the operation stack is determined by the query. The same
operations can be folded as a flat task summary, a fixed-session tree, a
semantic phase/action hierarchy, or a dataset-native trajectory.
Changing the fields changes the aggregation without changing the data.

This directly addresses the fixed-hierarchy problem from
\S\ref{sec:background}: sessions and spans are optional operation fields,
not structural skeleton nodes. Including \texttt{session} in the stack
produces a per-session drilldown (equivalent to a trace tree); excluding
it produces a cross-session aggregate (which no existing trace tool
provides). The same data supports both debugging and profiling views.

A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$: a predicate $\varphi$
selects which operations participate, a stack function $\sigma$ maps each
operation to a frame sequence, and a weight function $w$ assigns a
nonnegative measure. The view formalism supports arbitrary user-defined
views; four built-in defaults (Table~\ref{tab:views}) answer common
questions:

\begin{table}[t]

but selects different activities, stack structures, and weights.}
\label{tab:views}
\begin{tabular}{llll}
\toprule
View & $\varphi$ (select) & $w$ (width) & Question \\
\midrule
\texttt{tokens} & LLM calls & token count & Budget distribution? \\
\texttt{time} & All timed ops & duration (s) & Time distribution? \\
\texttt{files} & File-effect ops & event count & Repo coverage? \\

\subsection{Intent Recognition (R3: Deterministic Labels)}
\label{sec:intent}

Operations and stacks handle heterogeneity and flexible aggregation, but
folding still requires deterministic frame labels---the precondition
that agent prompts violate (\S\ref{sec:background}). \toolname solves
this through \emph{intent recognition}: mapping free-form prompts to
short, stable labels before stack construction.

The design uses a pluggable tagger framework with three backends:

\paragraph{Regex rules with agent-assisted iteration.}
The production default. Rules have the form
\texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative: run \toolname,
observe the unmatched rate and sample prompts, add rules, re-run, and
iterate until unmatched drops below 5\%. This typically takes 5--10
rounds. The resulting rule set is deterministic, reproducible, and
version-controllable.

\paragraph{Local LLM tagger.}
For exploration or complex multilingual prompts, a local model
(e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via llama.cpp) generates a single-word label
per prompt. Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity.
Labels are cached, so re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.

\paragraph{Unsupervised clustering.}
TF-IDF vectorization followed by K-Means discovers natural prompt groups
without predefined rules, feeding rule authoring.

The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
short because long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
and aggregation, not correctness verdicts.

\subsection{Mapping for Structured Traces}

For public benchmark datasets and structured trace formats, prompts are
already structured: action types, tool names, environment labels, and
quality annotations are explicit fields. \toolname supports deterministic
\emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from existing ones
before stack construction. A \emph{profile spec} records the complete
analysis configuration---data sources, mappings, predicates, stack
fields, and outputs---for deterministic replay.

This dual path explains why \toolname handles both real agent sessions
(which need intent recognition) and public benchmark traces (which need
mapping rules): both paths produce operations with fields, and the
stack query works identically on both.

\section{Implementation}
\label{sec:impl}

\toolname is implemented as a Rust CLI (Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}).
The \texttt{agent-session} crate reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
history files and reconstructs prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and
their triggered file and network effects. Each prompt opens a span. LLM
calls, tool calls, and system effects within that span inherit its
semantic label, connecting intent to system behavior without runtime
instrumentation. Public benchmark datasets enter as operation JSONL with
mapping rules deriving fields before stack construction. Standard Chrome
Trace Event format can also be imported, with non-\toolname protocol
fields preserved as operation fields.

Output formats include pprof protobuf (compatible with
\texttt{go tool pprof -http}), folded-stack text (compatible with
\texttt{flamegraph.pl}), standalone SVG flame graphs, and JSON summaries.
All outputs are deterministic given the same input and profile spec.

\toolname is the offline profiling component of the AgentSight
observability framework. AgentSight provides real-time eBPF-based
capture of SSL traffic, process events, and file/network effects.
\toolname aggregates the recorded traces into semantic profiles. The two
are complementary: AgentSight answers ``what happened during this run''
(debugging), \toolname answers ``where did the budget go across runs''
(profiling).

\subsection{RQ1: Does Semantic Profiling Separate What Flat Views Mix?}

The strongest argument against semantic profiling is that traditional
tools ``can already see the same information.'' RQ1 tests this claim
directly by measuring how much system-effect weight falls into
\emph{mixed-intent} buckets---buckets containing observations from
multiple semantic regions---under different projection choices.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Semantic-axis ablation on 183{,}714 system observations
from 325 real sessions. All rows preserve the same total weight.}
\label{tab:mixing}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
Projection & Unique stacks & Mixed wt.\% & Residual\% \\
\midrule
No semantic labels & 11{,}967 & 90.4 & 44.7 \\
Session label only & 15{,}027 & 84.4 & 33.4 \\
Prompt label only & 24{,}703 & 36.7 & 7.5 \\
Session + prompt & 26{,}829 & 0.0 & 0.0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:mixing} shows the result on 325 real Codex/Claude
sessions. Without semantic labels, 90.4\% of system-effect weight falls
into mixed buckets: a flat \texttt{cargo~test} counter shows 2{,}903
executions but cannot distinguish whether they came from
\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{refactor}, or \texttt{test}
prompts. Adding only the prompt label reduces mixed weight to 36.7\% and
residual to 7.5\%. The session label alone barely helps (84.4\%), because
sessions typically contain multiple intent phases.

A concrete example: \texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok}
appears under 48 distinct prompt tags. The top tag (\texttt{refactor})
accounts for only 32.0\%; the remaining 68.0\% comes from
\texttt{review}, \texttt{research}, \texttt{test}, \texttt{explain}, and
others. A flat summary or process audit merges all of these.

As a robustness check, a label-permutation test (1{,}000 shuffles within
each session) confirms the separation is not random ($p = 0.001$). The
primary evidence is the mixing reduction itself. The permutation test
verifies statistical significance. RQ3 evaluates label quality from a
complementary angle: agreement with ground-truth annotations on public
datasets.

RQ1 also tests whether query-time stack selection (R2) adds value
beyond flat label grouping. The same two-abstraction model covers all 15
public trace families (Table~\ref{tab:datasets}) without type-specific
objects. On the four oracle-rich families, the same 13{,}265 operations
fold from 9~dataset stacks to 57~phase stacks, 226~semantic stacks,
455~action stacks, or 3{,}757~fixed-session stacks by changing only the
stack fields. This is not achievable with a flat GROUP BY on a single
label: different stack depths answer different questions (task-level
budget vs.\ action-level duplication vs.\ session-level drilldown), and
the profiler produces all of them from the same operations.

The multi-view design is further validated by metric divergence. The
\texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views of the same sessions share
only 7/10 top prompt categories (Spearman $\rho = 0.623$).
\texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait) but 93rd by
tokens.

\subsection{RQ2: Can Profiler Groups Localize Hidden Labeled Problems?}

A profiler is useful if its top groups correspond to real problems: the
categories that concentrate failures, safety violations, or wasted
effort should appear at the top of the ranked output. RQ2 tests this
correspondence. The methodology is analogous to injecting known
bottlenecks in a CPU profiler evaluation: public benchmark datasets
provide ground-truth labels (failure, safety violation, redundant step,
human-task boundary); we hide these labels, run the profiler, rank the
resulting groups, and check whether the top groups contain the hidden
positives.

\paragraph{Benchmark setup.}
Six tasks across four datasets: AgentRewardBench looping and
side-effect, SATraj-OS unsafe operation, AgentNet incorrect and redundant
step, and OSWorld-Human group start. Together: 34{,}539 operations,
3{,}699 positives. Six views (flat, fixed-session, dataset-native,
raw-action, operation-stack, label-drilldown) and four rankers (width,
visible-risk, query-aware, oracle).

\paragraph{Localization results.}

Policy & Hidden & AP & R@5 & F1@5 & Work@5 & R@30\% & WTFP & Groups \\

Table~\ref{tab:localization} summarizes the results. Flat summaries
recover all positives but require inspecting everything
(Work@5\,=\,1.0). Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive quickly
(WTFP\,=\,0.004) but fragments the workload into 285 groups with only
2.3\% top-five recall. Operation-stack query-aware profiling inspects
9.4\% of the work in the top five groups, achieves 39.0\% budget-30
recall, and reduces groups to 157.5.

The result is a Pareto tradeoff, not dominance. The comparison also
serves as evidence for the two-abstraction model (C1): fixed-session
drilldown and dataset-native hierarchy are alternative abstractions that
fix the hierarchy at session or dataset boundaries. Operation stacks
subsume both as special cases (include \texttt{session} in the stack
to recover fixed-session; include \texttt{dataset} to recover
dataset-native). On localization, operation stacks improve top-five
recall over fixed-session on 5/6 tasks, reduce median group count by
45\%, and save 90\% of inspection work versus flat summaries.
Fixed-session drilldown retains lower work-to-first-positive on 4/6
tasks: profilers and debuggers are complementary.

Statistical validation supports these comparisons: bootstrap
(10{,}000 resamples) and label-permutation (2{,}000 trials) confirm
stable AP deltas exceeding the 95\% prevalence/group-size null on all
six tasks.

\paragraph{Actionability: which configuration knobs explain the results?}

Executable profile-spec patches modify stack fields, mapping rules, or
rankers, then re-run over the same visible operations. Five of six
patches improve AP, top-five lift, and first-positive work (median AP
delta 0.038, median top-five lift delta 0.575). Three reusable patterns
emerge: (1)~safety/side-effect tasks benefit from field and ranker
changes; (2)~step-quality tasks benefit from operation-stack
localization followed by fixed-session drilldown for examples;
(3)~human-boundary tasks require boundary-derived fields. The rejected
OSWorld-Human patch shows that visible rank features alone are
insufficient for boundary objectives; folding held-out boundary-derived
fields improves AP from 0.240 to 0.258 and reduces groups from 108 to
74, with an explicit work tradeoff.

Rank-feature ablations identify 7 critical feature rows
(\texttt{repeat\_signal}, write-action, \texttt{status=success}) and 3
misleading rows. Guided repairs improve AP on 2/3 misleading cases but
use offline scored feedback, not an automatic learned ranker.

\subsection{RQ3: How Reliable Is Intent Recognition?}

RQ1 and RQ2 assume that semantic labels are useful. RQ3 tests the
label-derivation pipeline itself. For structured traces (public
datasets), we evaluate the \emph{mapping} path against ground-truth
annotations. For free-form traces (real sessions), we evaluate the
\emph{intent-recognition} path at the scale and syntax level; quality
assessment of the LLM/regex tagger against free-form ground truth
remains future work.

\paragraph{Scale and syntax validity.}
On 325 real sessions, the LLM tagger processes 118{,}021 tag requests
(2{,}859 prompt rows, 114{,}837 LLM-call events). Of these, 82{,}886
hit the label cache; 35{,}136 are real llama.cpp calls to a local
3B-parameter model. Final tag failures: 0. On a fixed set of 300
redacted fragments, three model sizes (0.6B, 1.1B, 3B) all produce
900/900 syntactically valid outputs; p95 latencies are 23, 18, and
31\,ms respectively.

\paragraph{Ground-truth agreement on public datasets.}
Public benchmark datasets provide native action labels that serve as
ground truth for mapping quality. We run a leave-dataset-out evaluation:
for each of 9 datasets, we train mapping rules on the other 8 and
measure V-measure between the mapping-derived \texttt{phase} field and
the dataset's native \texttt{action} labels, plus boundary F1 between
mapped phase boundaries and native action boundaries.

Table~\ref{tab:vmeasure} shows the results. On 7/9 datasets, V-measure

A supervised boundary-derivation backend further validates the field
pipeline. On OSWorld-Human held-out adjacent pairs, a learned boundary
predictor achieves F1~0.77, beating the best simple baseline
(\texttt{always\_boundary}, F1~0.71). Learned backends beat simple
baselines on 4/5 tested boundary families, while AgentRewardBench
looping is fully explained by \texttt{repeat\_signal\_change} (baseline
F1~1.0). This supports field derivation as a guarded configuration
step, not automatic intent discovery.

\paragraph{Cross-configuration consistency.}
Two mapping-rule variants (differing in API/tool phase precedence) run
on the same 13{,}265 operations produce identical V-measure on 7/9
datasets; the two divergent datasets (api-bank, toolbench) differ by
$\leq$0.17 in V-measure. This suggests that mapping quality is robust
to minor rule variations on well-covered action vocabularies. Direct
cross-backend comparison between the regex and LLM taggers on the same
free-form prompts remains future work.

\paragraph{Semantic quality versus syntactic validity.}
Syntactic validity does not imply semantic quality. TinyLlama 1.1B
achieves high exact-stability (279/300 identical across repeats) but
concentrates on a narrow label set, outputting
\texttt{localization}/\texttt{localized} disproportionately. The 3B
model produces a broader vocabulary (328 unique prompt tags) but includes
noisy entries (\texttt{agentsightsm}, \texttt{testcodex}). A
display-governance pipeline reduces unique tags from 1{,}546 to 1{,}364
through deterministic aliases, raising top-20 support coverage from
93.7\% to 95.2\% without overwriting raw tags. This pipeline manages
noise but does not establish semantic adequacy---that is what the
ground-truth and cross-backend checks above provide.

\subsection{Case Studies}

RQ1--RQ3 evaluate mechanism and fidelity quantitatively. This subsection

\paragraph{Budget distribution.}
The \texttt{tokens} view (Figure~\ref{fig:flamegraphs}) reveals that
\texttt{review}-tagged prompts dominate the model budget, followed by

each category: under \texttt{prompt:review}, the dominant sub-frames are

The \texttt{files} view shows \texttt{debug}-tagged prompts across
different sessions repeatedly accessing the same source files under
\texttt{collector/src/}. The flame graph aggregates these into a single
wide bar; a timeline shows each as an isolated event.

\paragraph{Metric divergence.}
The \texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views share only 7/10 top prompt
categories. \texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait)
but 93rd by tokens; \texttt{benchmark} prompts show the reverse.

\paragraph{Path and network auditing.}
The \texttt{network} view attributes domain contacts to prompt
categories (\texttt{anthropic.com}, \texttt{crates.io},
\texttt{github.com}). The \texttt{files} view identifies accesses
outside the project root (\texttt{external/home},

\section{Related Work}

\textbf{Profiling and flame graphs.}
Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and pprof~\cite{pprof} establish the
folded-stack lineage: profiles are weighted samples with location
hierarchies. Pprof supports sample labels and can visualize them as
pseudo stack frames through tag-root/tag-leaf options. Perfetto
generalizes trace ingestion with SQL-based analysis and derived
events~\cite{perfetto}. These systems support query-time aggregation, so
\toolname does not claim novelty for flexible aggregation alone. The
difference is the domain: samples are agent operations, frames are
semantic labels derived from natural-language prompts through intent
recognition, and the evaluation scores profiler output against hidden
agent-trajectory labels.

\textbf{Agent tracing and LLM observability.}
OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI
spans~\cite{otel, openinference}. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, and Phoenix~\cite{phoenix} provide trace
visualization, session management, evaluations, and dashboards.
AgentOps~\cite{agentops} argues for structured agent observability
covering goals, plans, tools, and artifacts. These systems excel at
single-execution debugging: timeline views, span trees, and waterfall
charts help locate a specific failure. \toolname complements them with
cross-session aggregate profiling.
Datadog LLM Observability adds topic clustering over user messages, and
Laminar Signals extracts structured events from traces. These are steps
toward semantic aggregation, but they characterize \emph{input
distributions} (``30\% of users ask code questions''), not
\emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks consume 40\% of the
token budget''). \toolname produces the latter through folded-stack
aggregation where width represents cost.

\textbf{Agent failure diagnosis.}
AgentRx~\cite{agentrx} releases annotated failure trajectories and uses
constraint checking plus an LLM judge for root-cause localization.
TELBench~\cite{telbench} builds span-localization benchmarks from
semantic error annotations. AgentAtlas argues that outcome leaderboards
miss trajectory-level quality. These systems perform \emph{span-level}
fault localization within a single execution: which step failed and why.
\toolname performs \emph{category-level} aggregate profiling: which
categories of work produce the most failures, consume the most budget,
or generate repeated system effects across sessions.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Discussion}

\paragraph{Profiler and debugger are complementary.}
Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive faster on 4/6 tasks
(RQ2). This is expected: debuggers are designed for single-case
investigation. The profiler identifies \emph{which categories} deserve
attention; the debugger explains \emph{what happened} in a specific
case. \toolname supports both by including or excluding session fields in
the stack query. A typical workflow starts with the profiler (``review
tasks dominate the budget''), then drills into individual sessions to
understand why.

\paragraph{Agent-as-consumer.}
The profiler's structured output (JSON, pprof, folded stacks) is
designed to be consumed by automated analysis agents, not only human
developers. The RQ2 ranker strategies demonstrate this pattern: a
scoring policy reads profiler output, ranks groups by visible features,
and identifies high-cost or high-failure categories. In practice, an AI
coding agent can run \texttt{agentpprof --format json}, parse the output,
and recommend configuration changes---the same workflow that the
regex-rule iteration (\S\ref{sec:intent}) already uses. This positions
semantic profiling as infrastructure for agent self-diagnosis, not only
for human inspection.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
The real-session data (RQ1, RQ3, case studies) comes from one developer
on one project. RQ2 mitigates this with four independent public datasets
containing real agent traces from different research groups, but
multi-project and multi-user real-session evaluation would strengthen the
generality claim. The evaluation measures label-scored profiler fidelity,
not human or agent productivity. A controlled study comparing
flame-graph-guided diagnosis against timeline-based diagnosis would test
the practical value but is not required for the profiler-mechanism
contribution. \toolname currently reads Codex/Claude local histories and
operation JSONL; OpenTelemetry, LangSmith, and Langfuse trace imports are
engineering work, not design obstacles.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Conclusion}

Agent observability needs profiling, not only debugging. The obstacle is
that natural-language prompts lack the deterministic identifiers that
make flame-graph folding work. \toolname shows that two
abstractions---operations and operation stacks---close this gap once
intent recognition restores deterministic labels. The evaluation
confirms that semantic profiling separates information flat views merge,
localizes labeled problems with less work than both flat summaries and
fixed-session drilldown, and produces labels that agree with
ground-truth annotations across heterogeneous public datasets.

The main limitation is single-project real-session data; multi-project
evaluation and direct cross-backend tagger comparison are next steps.
The most impactful direction is trace-ecosystem integration:
importing OpenTelemetry and LangSmith traces as operations would let
\toolname profile any instrumented agent without a custom parser.

input.old_string:
\paragraph{Sessions are boundaries, not categories.}
A session groups events by execution, not by intent. A single session
may contain review, debugging, and refactoring phases. Splitting by
session assigns all of them to the same bucket. Conversely, two sessions
performing the same task produce two separate buckets that cannot be
merged without external logic.

\paragraph{Span names are not semantic labels.}
Span names describe mechanisms (\texttt{LLMCall}, \texttt{ToolInvoke},
\texttt{ChatCompletion}), not user intent (\texttt{review},
\texttt{debug}, \texttt{test}). Grouping by span name tells you how many
LLM calls occurred, not which categories of work consumed the budget.

\paragraph{Concrete example.}
In a real development project, the system effect
\texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok} appears 2{,}903 times
across 325 sessions. A flat process summary shows a single counter; no
existing trace tool can disaggregate these executions by the semantic
intent that triggered them. We quantify this disaggregation in
RQ1~(\S\ref{sec:eval}).

\subsection{Mapping for Structured Traces}

For public benchmark datasets and structured trace formats, prompts are
already structured: action types, tool names, environment labels, and
quality annotations are explicit fields. \toolname supports deterministic
\emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from existing ones
before stack construction. A \emph{profile spec} records the complete
analysis configuration---data sources, mappings, predicates, stack
fields, and outputs---for deterministic replay.

This dual path explains why \toolname handles both real agent sessions
(which need intent recognition) and public benchmark traces (which need
mapping rules): both paths produce operations with fields, and the
stack query works identically on both.

483	fold from 9~dataset stacks to 57~phase stacks, 226~semantic stacks,
484	455~action stacks, or 3{,}757~fixed-session stacks by changing only the
485	stack fields. This is not achievable with a flat GROUP BY on a single
486	label: different stack depths answer different questions (task-level
487	budget vs.\ action-level duplication vs.\ session-level drilldown), and
488	the profiler produces all of them from the same operations.
489	
490	The multi-view design is further validated by metric divergence. The
491	\texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views of the same sessions share
492	only 7/10 top prompt categories (Spearman $\rho = 0.623$).
493	\texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait) but 93rd by
494	tokens.
495	
496	%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
497	\subsection{RQ2: Can Profiler Groups Localize Hidden Labeled Problems?}
498	
499	A profiler is useful if its top groups correspond to real problems: the
500	categories that concentrate failures, safety violations, or wasted
501	effort should appear at the top of the ranked output. RQ2 tests this
502	correspondence. The methodology is analogous to injecting known
503	bottlenecks in a CPU profiler evaluation: public benchmark datasets
504	provide ground-truth labels (failure, safety violation, redundant step,
505	human-task boundary); we hide these labels, run the profiler, rank the
506	resulting groups, and check whether the top groups contain the hidden
507	positives.
508	
509	\paragraph{Benchmark setup.}
510	Six tasks across four datasets: AgentRewardBench looping and
511	side-effect, SATraj-OS unsafe operation, AgentNet incorrect and redundant
512	step, and OSWorld-Human group start. Together: 34{,}539 operations,
513	3{,}699 positives. Six views (flat, fixed-session, dataset-native,
514	raw-action, operation-stack, label-drilldown) and four rankers (width,
515	visible-risk, query-aware, oracle).
516	
517	\paragraph{Localization results.}
518	
519	\begin{table*}[t]
520	\centering\small
521	\caption{RQ2 hidden-label localization (medians across six tasks).
522	Hidden policies serve only as upper bounds. WTFP = work-to-first-positive.
523	``---'' = group count varies by task; no single median is reported.}
524	\label{tab:localization}
525	\begin{tabular}{lrrrrrrrr}
526	\toprule
527	Policy & Hidden & AP & R@5 & F1@5 & Work@5 & R@30\% & WTFP & Groups \\
528	\midrule
529	flat:width & 0 & 0.168 & 1.000 & 0.287 & 1.000 & 0.000 & 1.000 & 1.0 \\
530	fixed-session:query-aware & 0 & 0.348 & 0.023 & 0.043 & 0.016 & 0.356 & 0.004 & 285.0 \\
531	dataset-native:query-aware & 0 & 0.357 & 0.867 & 0.282 & 0.854 & 0.338 & 0.058 & --- \\
532	raw-action:query-aware & 0 & 0.274 & 0.244 & 0.220 & 0.151 & 0.333 & 0.037 & --- \\
533	op-stack:query-aware & 0 & 0.312 & 0.188 & 0.198 & 0.094 & 0.390 & 0.038 & 157.5 \\
534	op-stack:oracle-upper & 1 & 0.599 & 0.300 & 0.403 & 0.044 & 0.564 & 0.012 & --- \\
535	label-drilldown:oracle & 1 & 1.000 & 0.670 & 0.797 & 0.115 & 1.000 & 0.038 & --- \\
536	\bottomrule
537	\end{tabular}
538	\end{table*}
539	
540	Table~\ref{tab:localization} summarizes the results. Flat summaries
541	recover all positives but require inspecting everything
542	(Work@5\,=\,1.0). Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive quickly
543	(WTFP\,=\,0.004) but fragments the workload into 285 groups with only
544	2.3\% top-five recall. Operation-stack query-aware profiling inspects
545	9.4\% of the work in the top five groups, achieves 39.0\% budget-30
546	recall, and reduces groups to 157.5.
547	
548	The result is a Pareto tradeoff, not dominance. The comparison also
549	serves as evidence for the two-abstraction model (C1): fixed-session
550	drilldown and dataset-native hierarchy are alternative abstractions that
551	fix the hierarchy at session or dataset boundaries. Operation stacks
552	subsume both as special cases (include \texttt{session} in the stack
553	to recover fixed-session; include \texttt{dataset} to recover
554	dataset-native). On localization, operation stacks improve top-five
555	recall over fixed-session on 5/6 tasks, reduce median group count by
556	45\%, and save 90\% of inspection work versus flat summaries.
557	Fixed-session drilldown retains lower work-to-first-positive on 4/6
558	tasks: profilers and debuggers are complementary.
559	
560	Statistical validation supports these comparisons: bootstrap
561	(10{,}000 resamples) and label-permutation (2{,}000 trials) confirm
562	stable AP deltas exceeding the 95\% prevalence/group-size null on all
563	six tasks.
564	
565	\paragraph{Actionability: which configuration knobs explain the results?}
566	
567	Executable profile-spec patches modify stack fields, mapping rules, or
568	rankers, then re-run over the same visible operations. Five of six
569	patches improve AP, top-five lift, and first-positive work (median AP
570	delta 0.038, median top-five lift delta 0.575). Three reusable patterns
571	emerge: (1)~safety/side-effect tasks benefit from field and ranker
572	changes; (2)~step-quality tasks benefit from operation-stack
573	localization followed by fixed-session drilldown for examples;
574	(3)~human-boundary tasks require boundary-derived fields. The rejected
575	OSWorld-Human patch shows that visible rank features alone are
576	insufficient for boundary objectives; folding held-out boundary-derived
577	fields improves AP from 0.240 to 0.258 and reduces groups from 108 to
578	74, with an explicit work tradeoff.

674	%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
675	\subsection{Case Studies}
676	
677	RQ1--RQ3 evaluate mechanism and fidelity quantitatively. This subsection
678	demonstrates the aggregate, cross-session insights that motivate the
679	profiling abstraction---the kind of questions that per-event timeline
680	views structurally cannot answer. We profile the same 325-session
681	development project and report four representative observations.
682	
683	\paragraph{Budget distribution.}
684	The \texttt{tokens} view (Figure~\ref{fig:flamegraphs}) reveals that
685	\texttt{review}-tagged prompts dominate the model budget, followed by
686	\texttt{git}, \texttt{code}, \texttt{edit}, and \texttt{debug}. A
687	timeline of 80{,}000 individual LLM calls cannot produce this
688	distribution without external aggregation. The stack further decomposes
689	each category: under \texttt{prompt:review}, the dominant sub-frames are
690	\texttt{call:llm/code} and \texttt{call:llm/tool}.
691	
692	\paragraph{Cross-session duplication.}
693	The \texttt{files} view shows \texttt{debug}-tagged prompts across
694	different sessions repeatedly accessing the same source files under
695	\texttt{collector/src/}. The flame graph aggregates these into a single
696	wide bar; a timeline shows each as an isolated event.
697	
698	\paragraph{Metric divergence.}
699	The \texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views share only 7/10 top prompt
700	categories. \texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait)
701	but 93rd by tokens; \texttt{benchmark} prompts show the reverse.
702	
703	\paragraph{Path and network auditing.}
704	The \texttt{network} view attributes domain contacts to prompt
705	categories (\texttt{anthropic.com}, \texttt{crates.io},
706	\texttt{github.com}). The \texttt{files} view identifies accesses
707	outside the project root (\texttt{external/home},
708	\texttt{external/tmp}), supporting security auditing.
709	
710	\begin{figure}[t]
711	\centering
712	% \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/flamegraph-tokens.png}
713	\fbox{\parbox{0.93\linewidth}{\centering\small
714	[Flame-graph screenshots: tokens view (top) and files view (bottom)
715	showing budget distribution and file-access patterns across sessions]}}
716	\caption{Real flame graphs from a development project.
717	Top: \texttt{tokens} view (width = token count).
718	Bottom: \texttt{files} view (width = file-operation count).}
719	\Description{Two flame graphs showing token budget and file access
720	distribution across semantic prompt categories.}
721	\label{fig:flamegraphs}
722	\end{figure}
723	
724	%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
725	\subsection{Reproducibility}
726	
727	All results are backed by profile specs for deterministic replay. We
728	re-execute 76 tracked specs twice (152 invocations); all produce
729	identical semantic output. Median runtime: 1.6\,s per spec (p95:
730	2.8\,s). Deterministic-output mode stabilizes raw-byte output: 76/76
731	achieve both semantic and raw-byte determinism.
732	
733	%% ===================================================================
734	\section{Related Work}
735	
736	\textbf{Profiling and flame graphs.}
737	Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and pprof~\cite{pprof} establish the
738	folded-stack lineage: profiles are weighted samples with location
739	hierarchies. Pprof supports sample labels and can visualize them as
740	pseudo stack frames through tag-root/tag-leaf options. Perfetto
741	generalizes trace ingestion with SQL-based analysis and derived
742	events~\cite{perfetto}. These systems support query-time aggregation, so
743	\toolname does not claim novelty for flexible aggregation alone. The
744	difference is the domain: samples are agent operations, frames are
745	semantic labels derived from natural-language prompts through intent
746	recognition, and the evaluation scores profiler output against hidden
747	agent-trajectory labels.
748	
749	\textbf{Agent tracing and LLM observability.}
750	OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI
751	spans~\cite{otel, openinference}. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
752	Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, and Phoenix~\cite{phoenix} provide trace
753	visualization, session management, evaluations, and dashboards.
754	AgentOps~\cite{agentops} argues for structured agent observability
755	covering goals, plans, tools, and artifacts. These systems excel at
756	single-execution debugging: timeline views, span trees, and waterfall
757	charts help locate a specific failure. \toolname complements them with
758	cross-session aggregate profiling.
759	Datadog LLM Observability adds topic clustering over user messages, and
760	Laminar Signals extracts structured events from traces. These are steps
761	toward semantic aggregation, but they characterize \emph{input
762	distributions} (``30\% of users ask code questions''), not
763	\emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks consume 40\% of the
764	token budget''). \toolname produces the latter through folded-stack
765	aggregation where width represents cost.
766	
767	\textbf{Agent failure diagnosis.}
768	AgentRx~\cite{agentrx} releases annotated failure trajectories and uses
769	constraint checking plus an LLM judge for root-cause localization.
770	TELBench~\cite{telbench} builds span-localization benchmarks from
771	semantic error annotations. AgentAtlas argues that outcome leaderboards
772	miss trajectory-level quality. These systems perform \emph{span-level}
773	fault localization within a single execution: which step failed and why.
774	\toolname performs \emph{category-level} aggregate profiling: which
775	categories of work produce the most failures, consume the most budget,
776	or generate repeated system effects across sessions.
777	
778	%% ===================================================================
779	\section{Discussion}
780	
781	\paragraph{Profiler and debugger are complementary.}
782	Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive faster on 4/6 tasks
783	(RQ2). This is expected: debuggers are designed for single-case
784	investigation. The profiler identifies \emph{which categories} deserve
785	attention; the debugger explains \emph{what happened} in a specific
786	case. \toolname supports both by including or excluding session fields in
787	the stack query. A typical workflow starts with the profiler (``review
788	tasks dominate the budget''), then drills into individual sessions to
789	understand why.
790	
791	\paragraph{Agent-as-consumer.}
792	The profiler's structured output (JSON, pprof, folded stacks) is
793	designed to be consumed by automated analysis agents, not only human
794	developers. The RQ2 ranker strategies demonstrate this pattern: a
795	scoring policy reads profiler output, ranks groups by visible features,
796	and identifies high-cost or high-failure categories. In practice, an AI
797	coding agent can run \texttt{agentpprof --format json}, parse the output,
798	and recommend configuration changes---the same workflow that the
799	regex-rule iteration (\S\ref{sec:intent}) already uses. This positions
800	semantic profiling as infrastructure for agent self-diagnosis, not only
801	for human inspection.
802	
803	\paragraph{Limitations.}
804	The real-session data (RQ1, RQ3, case studies) comes from one developer
805	on one project. RQ2 mitigates this with four independent public datasets
806	containing real agent traces from different research groups, but
807	multi-project and multi-user real-session evaluation would strengthen the
808	generality claim. The evaluation measures label-scored profiler fidelity,
809	not human or agent productivity. A controlled study comparing
810	flame-graph-guided diagnosis against timeline-based diagnosis would test
811	the practical value but is not required for the profiler-mechanism
812	contribution. \toolname currently reads Codex/Claude local histories and
813	operation JSONL; OpenTelemetry, LangSmith, and Langfuse trace imports are
814	engineering work, not design obstacles.
815	
816	%% ===================================================================
817	\section{Conclusion}
818	
819	Agent observability needs profiling, not only debugging. The obstacle is
820	that natural-language prompts lack the deterministic identifiers that
821	make flame-graph folding work. \toolname shows that two
822	abstractions---operations and operation stacks---close this gap once
823	intent recognition restores deterministic labels. The evaluation
824	confirms that semantic profiling separates information flat views merge,
825	localizes labeled problems with less work than both flat summaries and
826	fixed-session drilldown, and produces labels that agree with
827	ground-truth annotations across heterogeneous public datasets.
828	
829	The main limitation is single-project real-session data; multi-project
830	evaluation and direct cross-backend tagger comparison are next steps.
831	The most impactful direction is trace-ecosystem integration:
832	importing OpenTelemetry and LangSmith traces as operations would let
833	\toolname profile any instrumented agent without a custom parser.

%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Case Studies}

RQ1--RQ3 evaluate mechanism and fidelity quantitatively. This subsection
demonstrates the aggregate, cross-session insights that motivate the
profiling abstraction---the kind of questions that per-event timeline
views structurally cannot answer. We profile the same 325-session
development project and report four representative observations.

\paragraph{Budget distribution.}
The \texttt{tokens} view (Figure~\ref{fig:flamegraphs}) reveals that
\texttt{review}-tagged prompts dominate the model budget, followed by
\texttt{git}, \texttt{code}, \texttt{edit}, and \texttt{debug}. A
timeline of 80{,}000 individual LLM calls cannot produce this
distribution without external aggregation. The stack further decomposes
each category: under \texttt{prompt:review}, the dominant sub-frames are
\texttt{call:llm/code} and \texttt{call:llm/tool}.

\paragraph{Cross-session duplication.}
The \texttt{files} view shows \texttt{debug}-tagged prompts across
different sessions repeatedly accessing the same source files under
\texttt{collector/src/}. The flame graph aggregates these into a single
wide bar; a timeline shows each as an isolated event.

\paragraph{Metric divergence.}
The \texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views share only 7/10 top prompt
categories. \texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait)
but 93rd by tokens; \texttt{benchmark} prompts show the reverse.

\paragraph{Path and network auditing.}
The \texttt{network} view attributes domain contacts to prompt
categories (\texttt{anthropic.com}, \texttt{crates.io},
\texttt{github.com}). The \texttt{files} view identifies accesses
outside the project root (\texttt{external/home},
\texttt{external/tmp}), supporting security auditing.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
% \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/flamegraph-tokens.png}
\fbox{\parbox{0.93\linewidth}{\centering\small
[Flame-graph screenshots: tokens view (top) and files view (bottom)
showing budget distribution and file-access patterns across sessions]}}
\caption{Real flame graphs from a development project.
Top: \texttt{tokens} view (width = token count).
Bottom: \texttt{files} view (width = file-operation count).}
\Description{Two flame graphs showing token budget and file access
distribution across semantic prompt categories.}
\label{fig:flamegraphs}
\end{figure}

%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Reproducibility}

All results are backed by profile specs for deterministic replay. We
re-execute 76 tracked specs twice (152 invocations); all produce
identical semantic output. Median runtime: 1.6\,s per spec (p95:
2.8\,s). Deterministic-output mode stabilizes raw-byte output: 76/76
achieve both semantic and raw-byte determinism.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Related Work}

\textbf{Profiling and flame graphs.}
Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and pprof~\cite{pprof} establish the
folded-stack lineage: profiles are weighted samples with location
hierarchies. Pprof supports sample labels and can visualize them as
pseudo stack frames through tag-root/tag-leaf options. Perfetto
generalizes trace ingestion with SQL-based analysis and derived
events~\cite{perfetto}. These systems support query-time aggregation, so
\toolname does not claim novelty for flexible aggregation alone. The
difference is the domain: samples are agent operations, frames are
semantic labels derived from natural-language prompts through intent
recognition, and the evaluation scores profiler output against hidden
agent-trajectory labels.

\textbf{Agent tracing and LLM observability.}
OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI
spans~\cite{otel, openinference}. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, and Phoenix~\cite{phoenix} provide trace
visualization, session management, evaluations, and dashboards.
AgentOps~\cite{agentops} argues for structured agent observability
covering goals, plans, tools, and artifacts. These systems excel at
single-execution debugging: timeline views, span trees, and waterfall
charts help locate a specific failure. \toolname complements them with
cross-session aggregate profiling.
Datadog LLM Observability adds topic clustering over user messages, and
Laminar Signals extracts structured events from traces. These are steps
toward semantic aggregation, but they characterize \emph{input
distributions} (``30\% of users ask code questions''), not
\emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks consume 40\% of the
token budget''). \toolname produces the latter through folded-stack
aggregation where width represents cost.

\textbf{Agent failure diagnosis.}
AgentRx~\cite{agentrx} releases annotated failure trajectories and uses
constraint checking plus an LLM judge for root-cause localization.
TELBench~\cite{telbench} builds span-localization benchmarks from
semantic error annotations. AgentAtlas argues that outcome leaderboards
miss trajectory-level quality. These systems perform \emph{span-level}
fault localization within a single execution: which step failed and why.
\toolname performs \emph{category-level} aggregate profiling: which
categories of work produce the most failures, consume the most budget,
or generate repeated system effects across sessions.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Discussion}

\paragraph{Profiler and debugger are complementary.}
Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive faster on 4/6 tasks
(RQ2). This is expected: debuggers are designed for single-case
investigation. The profiler identifies \emph{which categories} deserve
attention; the debugger explains \emph{what happened} in a specific
case. \toolname supports both by including or excluding session fields in
the stack query. A typical workflow starts with the profiler (``review
tasks dominate the budget''), then drills into individual sessions to
understand why.

\paragraph{Agent-as-consumer.}
The profiler's structured output (JSON, pprof, folded stacks) is
designed to be consumed by automated analysis agents, not only human
developers. The RQ2 ranker strategies demonstrate this pattern: a
scoring policy reads profiler output, ranks groups by visible features,
and identifies high-cost or high-failure categories. In practice, an AI
coding agent can run \texttt{agentpprof --format json}, parse the output,
and recommend configuration changes---the same workflow that the
regex-rule iteration (\S\ref{sec:intent}) already uses. This positions
semantic profiling as infrastructure for agent self-diagnosis, not only
for human inspection.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
The real-session data (RQ1, RQ3, case studies) comes from one developer
on one project. RQ2 mitigates this with four independent public datasets
containing real agent traces from different research groups, but
multi-project and multi-user real-session evaluation would strengthen the
generality claim. The evaluation measures label-scored profiler fidelity,
not human or agent productivity. A controlled study comparing
flame-graph-guided diagnosis against timeline-based diagnosis would test
the practical value but is not required for the profiler-mechanism
contribution. \toolname currently reads Codex/Claude local histories and
operation JSONL; OpenTelemetry, LangSmith, and Langfuse trace imports are
engineering work, not design obstacles.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Conclusion}

Agent observability needs profiling, not only debugging. The obstacle is
that natural-language prompts lack the deterministic identifiers that
make flame-graph folding work. \toolname shows that two
abstractions---operations and operation stacks---close this gap once
intent recognition restores deterministic labels. The evaluation
confirms that semantic profiling separates information flat views merge,
localizes labeled problems with less work than both flat summaries and
fixed-session drilldown, and produces labels that agree with
ground-truth annotations across heterogeneous public datasets.

The main limitation is single-project real-session data; multi-project
evaluation and direct cross-backend tagger comparison are next steps.
The most impactful direction is trace-ecosystem integration:
importing OpenTelemetry and LangSmith traces as operations would let
\toolname profile any instrumented agent without a custom parser.

### Must-fix

**MICRO-1: Abstract Beat 2 has a grammatical error — double "but" in one sentence.**
Line 33-35: "CPU flame graphs solve the equivalent aggregation problem for programs, **but** they rely on deterministic function names, **but** agent prompts are natural language and cannot be folded directly." Two independent-clause joins with "but" in sequence. The second "but" should be a different connective or the sentence should be split.

**Concrete fix:** Replace "but they rely on deterministic function names, but agent prompts" with "but they rely on deterministic function names. Agent prompts" — split into two sentences.

**MICRO-2: Intro ¶3 merges the insight (¶5 role) with the system description (¶6 role).**
Lines 86-100 pack three distinct roles into one paragraph: (1) the central insight ("agent observability requires profiling"), (2) the obstacle ("nondeterminism of natural-language identifiers"), and (3) the full system description (operations, stacks, intent recognition). The workshop template requires the same 7-paragraph structure as a full paper — insight and system must be separate paragraphs. Currently the intro has only 5 paragraphs (¶1 background+problem, ¶2 flame-graph analogy, ¶3 insight+system merged, ¶4 existing partial solutions, ¶5 contributions).

**Concrete fix:** Split lines 86-100 into two paragraphs. End the first at "natural-language identifiers." (the insight). Start the second with "This paper presents \toolname..." (the system). This restores ¶5 (insight) and ¶6 (this paper) as distinct paragraphs.

**MICRO-3: Intro is missing ¶3 (root cause) and ¶4 (existing solutions fail) as distinct paragraphs.**
The current intro has ¶1 (background+problem merged), ¶2 (flame-graph analogy = partial root cause), then jumps to ¶3 (insight+system). The template requires: ¶1 background, ¶2 problem, ¶3 root cause, ¶4 existing solutions fail, ¶5 insight, ¶6 this paper, ¶7 contributions. The "existing solutions fail" content (¶4) is currently ¶4 in the text (lines 102-110, the Datadog/Laminar paragraph), which appears AFTER the system is described — it should come BEFORE the insight to build the argument: background → problem → root cause → existing solutions fail → insight → this paper.

**Concrete fix:** Move the Datadog/Laminar paragraph (lines 102-110) to before the insight paragraph. Then split ¶1 (lines 63-75): the first three sentences are background (¶1); the sentence starting "But no existing tool provides..." starts the problem (¶2). The flame-graph paragraph (lines 77-84) serves as root cause (¶3). This yields: ¶1 background, ¶2 problem, ¶3 root cause (flame graphs show the structural gap), ¶4 existing partial solutions (Datadog/Laminar), ¶5 insight, ¶6 this paper, ¶7 contributions.

---

### Should-fix

**MICRO-4: Evaluation setup paragraph (lines 391-410) is overloaded — mixes data description, reproducibility, and design claims.**
The setup paragraph carries three distinct ideas: (a) data sources, (b) what the data contains, and (c) reproducibility claims (profile-spec replay). Reproducibility is a separate concern from experimental setup. The sentence about 13,265 operations folding into different stacks (lines 405-410) is an RQ1-style claim, not setup.

**Concrete fix:** End the setup paragraph after "No source requires a type-specific profiler object" (line 404). Move the "13,265 operations fold into..." sentence to RQ1. Move the reproducibility sentence ("All results are backed by profile specs...") to the end of RQ3 or a brief closing paragraph of the evaluation.

**MICRO-5: RQ1 is too long — seven paragraphs spanning 75 lines (435-524).**
RQ1 contains: (1) framing, (2) table discussion, (3) concrete example, (4) robustness check, (5) query-time stack value, (6) metric divergence, (7) case-study aggregate insights. For a workshop paper, this makes RQ1 nearly as long as Design. Paragraphs 5-7 mix RQ1's original question ("does semantic profiling separate?") with secondary questions (multi-view value, concrete insights).

**Concrete fix:** Tighten paragraphs 5-7. The case-study paragraph (lines 499-510) can be compressed to 2-3 sentences since it illustrates rather than proves. The metric-divergence paragraph (lines 493-497) is only 4 sentences — consider folding it into the preceding paragraph about query-time stacks.

**MICRO-6: RQ2 opens with a generic statement rather than the specific question.**
Lines 529-530: "A profiler is useful if its top groups correspond to real problems." This is a general truism, not a topic sentence for the specific question being tested. The actual question appears mid-paragraph: "RQ2 tests this correspondence."

**Concrete fix:** Lead with the specific question: "RQ2 asks whether the profiler's top groups correspond to real labeled problems—whether categories that concentrate failures or wasted effort surface at the top of ranked output."

**MICRO-7: RQ3 has five `\paragraph{}` headers in a workshop paper.**
Lines 626, 635, 682, 691, and the boundary-derivation paragraph all use `\paragraph{}`. The common-pitfalls reference flags `\paragraph{}` as clutter in 6-8 page papers. Five of them in one subsection makes RQ3 read like a catalog of sub-experiments rather than a cohesive argument.

**Concrete fix:** Remove at least the "Cross-configuration consistency" and "Semantic quality versus syntactic validity" paragraph headers (lines 682, 691). These are supporting evidence that can flow as regular paragraphs under the main RQ3 narrative. Keep "Scale and syntax validity" and "Ground-truth agreement" if needed for navigation, but consider removing those too.

---

### Consider

**FLOW-1: Intro ¶1 topic sentence could be sharper.**
Line 63: "AI agent systems produce execution traces that interleave prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, process events, and benchmark labels." This is a factual observation but reads as a laundry list. A stronger topic sentence would foreground the domain significance.

**Concrete fix:** Consider: "AI agent systems produce heterogeneous execution traces spanning prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and system effects." Move the full enumeration to a later sentence.

**FLOW-2: Design §3.1 last sentence repeats the subsection title.**
Line 236-237: "This satisfies R1: the profiler does not need to distinguish event types at the object-model level." This echoes the opening sentence (line 225-226) almost verbatim.

**Concrete fix:** Drop the final sentence — the subsection heading already announces R1, and the content demonstrates it.

**FLOW-3: The "Note that" sentence in Design (lines 307-309) breaks the flow.**
"Note that \toolname is an offline, post-hoc profiler..." appears between the view-formalism table/figure block and the Intent Recognition subsection. It's a scope clarification, not a design decision.

**Concrete fix:** Move this to the first sentence of Implementation (§4), where the offline/post-hoc nature is contextually appropriate ("AgentSight provides real-time capture; \toolname is the offline profiling component").</result>

\title{AgentPProf: Semantic Profiling for AI Agent Traces}

\begin{abstract}
% Beat 1: Context
AI agents produce complex execution traces spanning prompts, LLM calls,
tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects. As deployments grow
to hundreds of sessions, both human operators and automated analysis
pipelines need aggregate views---not just per-execution debugging.

% Beat 2: Problem
Existing observability tools organize events into fixed session/span
hierarchies suited for single-run debugging but unable to fold events
across sessions by semantic work category. CPU flame graphs solve the
equivalent aggregation problem for programs, but they rely on
deterministic function names, but agent prompts are natural language and
cannot be folded directly.

% Beat 3: This paper
We show that agent profiling reduces to two abstractions once intent
recognition restores the deterministic-label precondition. An
\emph{operation} is a uniform weighted record for any agent activity; an
\emph{operation stack} is a field projection chosen at query time.
Sessions and spans become optional fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
\toolname implements this model with pluggable intent-recognition
backends (regex rules, local LLM tagging, unsupervised clustering) and
produces flame graphs, pprof profiles, and structured JSON consumable by
both developers and analysis agents.

% Beat 4: Results
On 325 real agent sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of
system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public datasets
(34{,}539 operations), operation-stack profiling reduces inspection work
by 90\% versus flat summaries and fragmentation by 45\% versus
fixed-session drilldown. Leave-dataset-out mapping achieves V-measure
above 0.7 on 7/9 held-out datasets.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

%% ===================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

AI agent systems produce execution traces that interleave prompts, LLM
calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, process events, and benchmark
labels. As agent deployments scale to hundreds of sessions and tens of
thousands of calls, both developers and automated analysis agents need
to answer aggregate questions: which categories of work consume the most
tokens, where do repeated failures concentrate, and how does cost
distribute across semantic task families? Existing observability
tools---LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel}---organize
events into per-execution timelines and span trees, enabling
single-run debugging. But no existing tool provides an aggregate view
that folds heterogeneous events across sessions into a cost or frequency
distribution grouped by semantic work category.

CPU profilers solved the equivalent problem for programs: flame
graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} fold millions of function-call samples into
a single chart where width represents cost. The key enabler is
\emph{deterministic} function names that merge identical call stacks.
Agent traces break this assumption---prompts are natural language, and
two prompts expressing the same intent share no characters. We develop
this gap and the design requirements it implies in
\S\ref{sec:background}.

The central insight is that agent observability requires
\emph{profiling}: aggregate, cross-session cost attribution grouped by
user intent---which we call \emph{semantic} to distinguish from
execution-structural groupings like sessions or spans. The obstacle to
applying classical profiler techniques is the nondeterminism of
natural-language identifiers. This paper presents \toolname, a profiler
that restores aggregate flame-graph analysis for agent traces. The
profiler is built on two abstractions: an \emph{operation} (a uniform
weighted record for any agent activity) and an \emph{operation stack}
(a field projection chosen at query time). Sessions, spans, and trace
identifiers are operation fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
\emph{Intent recognition}---mapping free-form prompts to stable labels
through pluggable backends (regex rules, local LLM tagging, or
unsupervised clustering)---restores the deterministic-label precondition
that flame-graph folding requires.

Some existing tools take steps toward semantic grouping: Datadog LLM
Observability clusters user messages by
topic,\footnote{\url{https://docs.datadoghq.com/llm_observability/}}
and Laminar extracts structured signals from
traces.\footnote{\url{https://docs.lmnr.ai/signals/introduction}} These tools characterize \emph{input
distributions} (``30\% of users ask code questions'') but not
\emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks consume 40\% of the
token budget''). \toolname produces the latter through folded-stack
aggregation where width represents cost.

This paper makes three contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Insight: agent profiling reduces to two abstractions.}
  We show that the aggregation gap in agent observability---fixed
  session/span hierarchies cannot fold by semantic category---is closed
  by combining uniform operation records with query-time stack
  projections, once intent recognition restores deterministic labels
  (\S\ref{sec:background}--\S\ref{sec:design}).
\item \textbf{System: \toolname.}
  We implement this model as a Rust CLI with pluggable intent
  recognition, four built-in views, and output formats (pprof, SVG,
  JSON) consumable by both developers and automated analysis agents
  (\S\ref{sec:impl}).
\item \textbf{Evaluation.}
  We show that semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight
  that unsemantic views merge (RQ1), that operation-stack profiling
  localizes hidden labeled problems with 90\% less work than flat
  summaries (RQ2), and that mapping-derived labels agree with
  ground-truth annotations on 7/9 public datasets (RQ3)
  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Evaluation}
\label{sec:eval}

We organize the evaluation around three research questions, followed by
case studies and a reproducibility check.

\paragraph{Evaluation setup.}
We use two classes of data. \emph{Real agent sessions}: 325 readable
local sessions (198~Codex, 50~Claude, 77~Claude subagent) from a
multi-month development project, containing 183{,}714 system
observations. \emph{Public labeled traces}: 15 families covering web,
mobile, desktop, software, API, and dialogue agents
(Table~\ref{tab:datasets}), totaling 47{,}590 operations through
mapping rules. All public traces are real agent or human executions
collected and labeled by their respective benchmark projects. Four
oracle-rich families (AgentRewardBench, SATraj-OS, AgentNet,
OSWorld-Human) provide hidden ground-truth labels for RQ2. No source
requires a type-specific profiler object: the same 13{,}265 operations
fold into 9~dataset stacks through 3{,}757~fixed-session stacks by
changing only the stack fields. All results are backed by profile specs
for deterministic replay: 76 tracked specs re-executed twice (152
invocations) produce identical output, with median runtime 1.6\,s per
spec.

\section{Conclusion}

Agent observability needs profiling, not only debugging. The obstacle is
that natural-language prompts lack the deterministic identifiers that
make flame-graph folding work. \toolname shows that two
abstractions---operations and operation stacks---close this gap once
intent recognition restores deterministic labels. The evaluation
confirms that semantic profiling separates information flat views merge,
localizes labeled problems with less work than both flat summaries and
fixed-session drilldown, and produces labels that agree with
ground-truth annotations across heterogeneous public datasets.

Profilers and debuggers are complementary: fixed-session drilldown finds
a first positive faster on 4/6 tasks (RQ2), while the profiler
identifies which categories deserve attention. \toolname supports both
by including or excluding session fields in the stack query. The
profiler's structured output (JSON, pprof, folded stacks) also enables
automated consumption: an analysis agent can run
\texttt{agentpprof --format json}, rank groups by visible features, and
recommend configuration changes, positioning semantic profiling as
infrastructure for agent self-diagnosis.

The real-session data comes from one developer on one project. RQ2
mitigates this with four independent public datasets, but multi-project
evaluation would strengthen the generality claim. The evaluation
measures profiler fidelity, not human productivity. The most impactful
next step is trace-ecosystem integration: importing OpenTelemetry and
LangSmith traces as operations would let \toolname profile any
instrumented agent without a custom parser.

671	Two mapping-rule variants (differing in API/tool phase precedence) run
672	on the same 13{,}265 operations and produce identical V-measure on 7/9
673	datasets, with the two divergent datasets differing by $\leq$0.17.
674	Mapping quality is robust to minor rule variations on well-covered
675	action vocabularies. Direct cross-backend comparison between the regex
676	and LLM taggers on the same free-form prompts remains future work.
677	
678	Syntactic validity does not imply semantic quality. TinyLlama 1.1B
679	achieves high exact-stability (279/300 identical across repeats) but
680	concentrates on a narrow label set. The 3B model produces a broader
681	vocabulary (328 unique prompt tags) but includes noisy entries. A
682	display-governance pipeline reduces unique tags from 1{,}546 to 1{,}364
683	through deterministic aliases, raising top-20 support coverage from
684	93.7\% to 95.2\% without overwriting raw tags. This pipeline manages
685	noise but does not establish semantic adequacy---that is what the
686	ground-truth and cross-backend checks above provide.
