\documentclass[sigconf]{acmart}

\setcopyright{none}
\settopmatter{printacmref=false}
\renewcommand\footnotetextcopyrightpermission[1]{}
\pagestyle{plain}

\usepackage{booktabs}
\usepackage{array}
\usepackage{xspace}
\usepackage{url}
\usepackage{graphicx}

\newcommand{\toolname}{\textsc{AgentPProf}\xspace}
\newcommand{\operation}{\texttt{operation}\xspace}
\newcommand{\opstack}{\texttt{operation stack}\xspace}

\begin{document}

\title{AgentPProf: Semantic Profiling for AI Agent Traces}

\begin{abstract}
% Beat 1: Context
AI agents produce complex execution traces spanning prompts, LLM calls,
tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects. As deployments grow
to hundreds of sessions, both human operators and automated analysis
pipelines need aggregate views---not just per-execution debugging.

% Beat 2: Problem
Existing observability tools organize events into fixed session/span
hierarchies suited for single-run debugging but unable to fold events
across sessions by semantic work category. CPU flame graphs solve the
equivalent aggregation problem for programs, but they rely on
deterministic function names. Agent prompts are natural language and
cannot be folded directly.

% Beat 3: This paper
We show that agent profiling reduces to two abstractions once intent
recognition restores the deterministic-label precondition. An
\emph{operation} is a uniform weighted record for any agent activity; an
\emph{operation stack} is a field projection chosen at query time.
Sessions and spans become optional fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
\toolname implements this model with pluggable intent-recognition
backends (regex rules, local LLM tagging, unsupervised clustering) and
produces flame graphs, pprof profiles, and structured JSON consumable by
both developers and analysis agents.

% Beat 4: Results
On 325 real agent sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of
system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public datasets
(34{,}539 operations), operation-stack profiling reduces inspection work
by 90\% versus flat summaries and fragmentation by 45\% versus
fixed-session drilldown. Leave-dataset-out mapping achieves V-measure
above 0.7 on 7/9 held-out datasets.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

%% ===================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

AI agent systems produce heterogeneous execution traces spanning
prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects.
As deployments scale to hundreds of sessions and tens of thousands of
calls, both developers and automated analysis agents need to answer
aggregate questions: which categories of work consume the most tokens,
where do repeated failures concentrate, and how does cost distribute
across semantic task families?

Existing observability tools---LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, OpenTelemetry
GenAI~\cite{otel}---organize events into per-execution timelines and
span trees, enabling single-run debugging. But no existing tool provides
an aggregate view that folds heterogeneous events across sessions into a
cost or frequency distribution grouped by semantic work category.

CPU profilers solved the equivalent problem for programs: flame
graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} fold millions of function-call samples into
a single chart where width represents cost. The key enabler is
\emph{deterministic} function names that merge identical call stacks.
Agent traces break this assumption---prompts are natural language, and
two prompts expressing the same intent share no characters. We develop
this gap and the design requirements it implies in
\S\ref{sec:background}.

Some existing tools take steps toward semantic grouping: Datadog LLM
Observability clusters user messages by
topic,\footnote{\url{https://docs.datadoghq.com/llm_observability/}}
and Laminar extracts structured signals from
traces.\footnote{\url{https://docs.lmnr.ai/signals/introduction}} These
tools characterize \emph{input distributions} (``30\% of users ask code
questions'') but not \emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks
consume 40\% of the token budget'').

The central insight is that agent observability requires
\emph{profiling}: aggregate, cross-session cost attribution grouped by
user intent---which we call \emph{semantic} to distinguish from
execution-structural groupings like sessions or spans. The obstacle to
applying classical profiler techniques is the nondeterminism of
natural-language identifiers.

This paper presents \toolname, a profiler that restores aggregate
flame-graph analysis for agent traces. The profiler is built on two
abstractions: an \emph{operation} (a uniform weighted record for any
agent activity) and an \emph{operation stack} (a field projection chosen
at query time). Sessions, spans, and trace identifiers are operation
fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes. \emph{Intent recognition}---mapping
free-form prompts to stable labels through pluggable backends (regex
rules, local LLM tagging, or unsupervised clustering)---restores the
deterministic-label precondition that flame-graph folding requires.

This paper makes three contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Insight: agent profiling reduces to two abstractions.}
  We show that the aggregation gap in agent observability---fixed
  session/span hierarchies cannot fold by semantic category---is closed
  by combining uniform operation records with query-time stack
  projections, once intent recognition restores deterministic labels
  (\S\ref{sec:background}--\S\ref{sec:design}).
\item \textbf{System: \toolname.}
  We implement this model as a Rust CLI with pluggable intent
  recognition, four built-in views, and output formats (pprof, SVG,
  JSON) consumable by both developers and automated analysis agents
  (\S\ref{sec:impl}).
\item \textbf{Evaluation.}
  We show that semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight
  that unsemantic views merge (RQ1), that operation-stack profiling
  localizes hidden labeled problems with 90\% less work than flat
  summaries (RQ2), and that mapping-derived labels agree with
  ground-truth annotations on 7/9 public datasets (RQ3)
  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
\end{enumerate}

# Workshop Paper (6 pages)

AgenticOS, HotOS, WORDS, APSys, and similar workshops.

Abstract and Introduction follow the SAME structure as a full paper.
Body sections are compressed. This file lists only the differences from `full-paper-12p.md`.

---

## Abstract

Same as full paper: 1 paragraph, 150-250 words, same sentence roles.

---

## 1. Introduction (~1 page)

Same 7-paragraph structure as a full paper. Same roles, same order, same rules. Do NOT merge paragraphs. Each paragraph is shorter (2-3 sentences instead of 3-5), but all 7 are present:

- ¶1: Background + Context
- ¶2: Problem + example
- ¶3: Root cause
- ¶4: Existing solutions fail
- ¶5: Key insight
- ¶6: This paper + numbers
- ¶7: Contributions (2-3 items instead of 3-4)

Same topic-sentence rule: every paragraph's first sentence is the topic sentence. Transitions go at the start of the new paragraph.

---

## Differences from Full Paper

### No separate Background and Motivation sections
- Merged into one section: "Background and Motivation"
- 2-3 subsections
- Background concepts folded into the motivation narrative

### No separate Overview section
- The Design section opening paragraph serves as overview
- Architecture diagram, if present, goes in Design (not a separate section)
- Walk-through of the architecture is 1 paragraph, not a full section

### Design (~1-1.5 pages, 2-3 subsections)
- Opening paragraph covers both design goals AND system overview
- Fewer subsections (2-3 instead of 3-5)
- Each subsection can be shorter (1 paragraph of design + 1 paragraph of mechanism)
- Design and implementation MAY be partially merged if space demands

### Implementation (~0.5-1 page)
- May be merged with Design as "Design and Implementation"
- If separate, fewer subsections (2-3)
- Code size and integration in final paragraph

### Evaluation (~1-1.5 pages)
- Setup paragraph (shorter)
- 2-3 experiments (instead of 3-5)
- Limitations at the end of eval (not a separate subsection — can be final paragraph)

### No separate Discussion section
- Future directions folded into Conclusion or Limitations
- Broader impact mentioned in 1-2 sentences if at all

### Related Work (~0.5 page)
- 3-4 topic groups (instead of 3-5)
- Each group shorter (3-4 sentences instead of 5-7)

### Conclusion (~0.25 page)
- Same structure as full paper
- May include 1 sentence of future work (since there's no Discussion section)

input.old_string:
\begin{abstract}
% Beat 1: Context
AI agents produce complex execution traces spanning prompts, LLM calls,
tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects. As deployments grow
to hundreds of sessions, both human operators and automated analysis
pipelines need aggregate views---not just per-execution debugging.

% Beat 2: Problem
Existing observability tools organize events into fixed session/span
hierarchies suited for single-run debugging but unable to fold events
across sessions by semantic work category. CPU flame graphs solve the
equivalent aggregation problem for programs, but they rely on
deterministic function names. Agent prompts are natural language and
cannot be folded directly.

% Beat 3: This paper
We show that agent profiling reduces to two abstractions once intent
recognition restores the deterministic-label precondition. An
\emph{operation} is a uniform weighted record for any agent activity; an
\emph{operation stack} is a field projection chosen at query time.
Sessions and spans become optional fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
\toolname implements this model with pluggable intent-recognition
backends (regex rules, local LLM tagging, unsupervised clustering) and
produces flame graphs, pprof profiles, and structured JSON consumable by
both developers and analysis agents.

% Beat 4: Results
On 325 real agent sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of
system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public datasets
(34{,}539 operations), operation-stack profiling reduces inspection work
by 90\% versus flat summaries and fragmentation by 45\% versus
fixed-session drilldown. Leave-dataset-out mapping achieves V-measure
above 0.7 on 7/9 held-out datasets.
\end{abstract}

## Round 3 — Logic Flow Review

### 1. Section role

This is the complete paper (6 pages, workshop format). The review focuses on whether the argument flows coherently from intro through body to conclusion, whether claims are supported, and whether logic gaps exist. Overall: the story is consistent—intro, background, design, eval, and conclusion tell the same profiling-vs-debugging narrative. The main logic issues are (a) a circular dependency between the claimed insight and its evidence, (b) RQ1 overreach into qualitative claims it doesn't test, and (c) an evaluation that conflates two different notions of "profiling works."

### 2. Top issues ranked by severity

1. **Major / logic-organization — RQ1 scope creep: seven paragraphs serve three different purposes.** RQ1 is titled "Does semantic profiling separate what flat views mix?" The first three paragraphs (mixing table, concrete example, permutation test) answer this question. But paragraphs 4–7 shift to demonstrating query-time stack flexibility (R2 coverage test), metric divergence across views, and qualitative case-study insights (budget distribution, cross-session duplication, security auditing). These are distinct claims that lack the quantitative framing of the RQ. A reviewer would ask: "Is RQ1 one question or three? The mixing metric is clean, but the case-study paragraph is a qualitative demo, not a measurement."

2. **Major / logic-organization — Circular dependency: insight claims labels are useful, RQ1 measures separation assuming labels are correct.** The intro ¶5 claims the insight is that "agent observability requires profiling." RQ1 then shows that adding prompt labels reduces mixing from 90% to 37%. But RQ1 uses the author's own regex-derived labels as the semantic axis. The paper acknowledges this: "RQ3 evaluates label quality from a complementary angle." AI agents produce complex execution traces spanning prompts, LLM calls,
tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects; as deployments grow
to hundreds of sessions, both human operators and automated analysis
pipelines need aggregate views, not just per-execution debugging.

hierarchies suited for single-run debugging but unable to fold events
across sessions by semantic work category.

recognition restores the deterministic-label precondition that
flame-graph folding requires.

both developers and analysis agents.

system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public datasets
(34{,}539 operations), operation-stack profiling reduces inspection work
by 90\% versus flat summaries and fragmentation by 45\% versus

\documentclass[sigconf]{acmart}

\setcopyright{none}
\settopmatter{printacmref=false}
\renewcommand\footnotetextcopyrightpermission[1]{}
\pagestyle{plain}

\usepackage{booktabs}
\usepackage{array}
\usepackage{xspace}
\usepackage{url}
\usepackage{graphicx}

\newcommand{\toolname}{\textsc{AgentPProf}\xspace}
\newcommand{\operation}{\texttt{operation}\xspace}
\newcommand{\opstack}{\texttt{operation stack}\xspace}

\begin{document}

\title{AgentPProf: Semantic Profiling for AI Agent Traces}

\begin{abstract}
AI agents produce complex execution traces spanning prompts, LLM calls,
tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects. As deployments grow
to hundreds of sessions, both human operators and automated analysis
pipelines need aggregate views, not just per-execution debugging.
Existing observability tools organize events into fixed session/span
hierarchies suited for single-run debugging but unable to fold events
across sessions by semantic work category.
We show that agent profiling reduces to two abstractions once intent
recognition restores the deterministic-label precondition that
flame-graph folding requires.
An \emph{operation} is a uniform weighted record for any agent activity;
an \emph{operation stack} is a field projection chosen at query time.
\toolname implements this model with pluggable intent-recognition
backends (regex rules, local LLM tagging, unsupervised clustering) and
produces flame graphs, pprof profiles, and structured JSON consumable by
both developers and analysis agents.
On 325 real agent sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of
system-effect weight that flat views merge. On six localization tasks across four public datasets
(34{,}539 operations), operation-stack profiling reduces inspection work
by 90\% versus flat summaries and group fragmentation by 45\% versus
fixed-session drilldown. Leave-dataset-out mapping achieves V-measure
above 0.7 on 7/9 held-out datasets.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

%% ===================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

%% ¶1: Background + Context
AI agent systems produce heterogeneous execution traces spanning
prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects.
As deployments scale to hundreds of sessions and tens of thousands of
calls, both developers and automated analysis agents need aggregate
views: which categories of work consume the most tokens, where do
failures concentrate, and how does cost distribute across semantic task
families?

%% ¶2: Problem + example
However, existing observability tools---LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, OpenTelemetry
GenAI~\cite{otel}---organize events into per-execution timelines and
span trees, enabling single-run debugging but not cross-session
aggregation. In a real development project, the system effect
\texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok} appears 2{,}903 times
across 325 sessions, yet no existing trace tool can disaggregate these
executions by the semantic intent that triggered them.

%% ¶3: Root cause
CPU profilers solved the equivalent aggregation problem for programs:
flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} fold millions of function-call samples
into a single chart where width represents cost. The key enabler is
\emph{deterministic} function names that merge identical call stacks.
Agent traces break this precondition---prompts are natural language, and
two prompts expressing the same intent share no characters
(\S\ref{sec:background}).

%% ¶4: Existing solutions fail
Some existing tools take steps toward semantic grouping: Datadog LLM
Observability clusters user messages by
topic,\footnote{\url{https://docs.datadoghq.com/llm_observability/}}
and Laminar extracts structured signals from
traces.\footnote{\url{https://docs.lmnr.ai/signals/introduction}} These
tools characterize \emph{input distributions} (``30\% of users ask code
questions'') but not \emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks
consume 40\% of the token budget'').

%% ¶5: Key insight
We observe that agent observability requires \emph{profiling}---aggregate,
cross-session cost attribution grouped by user intent, which we call
\emph{semantic} to distinguish from execution-structural groupings like
sessions or spans. The obstacle is the nondeterminism of
natural-language identifiers, but this obstacle can be removed through
intent recognition that restores deterministic labels.

%% ¶6: This paper + numbers
This paper presents \toolname, a profiler that restores aggregate
flame-graph analysis for agent traces. The profiler is built on two
abstractions: an \emph{operation} (a uniform weighted record for any
agent activity) and an \emph{operation stack} (a field projection chosen
at query time). \emph{Intent recognition}---mapping free-form prompts to
stable labels through pluggable backends (regex rules, local LLM
tagging, or unsupervised clustering)---restores the deterministic-label
precondition. On 325 real sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of
system-effect weight that flat views merge; on four public datasets,
operation-stack profiling reduces inspection work by 90\% versus flat
summaries.

%% ¶7: Contributions
This paper makes three contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Insight: agent profiling reduces to two abstractions.}
  We show that the aggregation gap in agent observability---fixed
  session/span hierarchies cannot fold by semantic category---is closed
  by combining uniform operation records with query-time stack
  projections, once intent recognition restores deterministic labels

140	
141	\subsection{How Existing Agent Trace Models Work}
142	
143	Current agent observability tools organize traces around fixed
144	hierarchies. OpenTelemetry represents an execution as a \emph{trace}
145	containing a tree of \emph{spans}, each with a name, duration, and
146	key-value attributes. LangSmith and Langfuse group spans into
147	\emph{sessions} and display them as timelines or waterfall charts.
148	Phoenix and OpenInference add GenAI-specific span types for LLM calls,
149	tool invocations, retrieval steps, and agent reasoning.
150	
151	These models share a structural property: the session or span tree is the
152	skeleton of the data. Every event belongs to exactly one span, and spans
153	nest in a fixed parent-child hierarchy determined at execution time.
154	This design is effective for debugging: a developer can locate a failing
155	span, inspect its attributes, and trace its parent chain to understand
156	the execution context.
157	
158	\subsection{Why Fixed Hierarchies Cannot Profile}
159	
160	Profiling requires a fundamentally different operation: \emph{folding}
161	events across executions by semantic category so that width represents
162	aggregate cost. Fixed session/span hierarchies obstruct this in three
163	ways.
164	
165	First, sessions are boundaries, not categories: a single session may
166	contain review, debugging, and refactoring phases, and splitting by
167	session assigns all of them to the same bucket. Conversely, two sessions
168	performing the same task produce separate buckets that cannot be merged
169	without external logic. Second, span names describe mechanisms
170	(\texttt{LLMCall}, \texttt{ToolInvoke}, \texttt{ChatCompletion}), not
171	user intent (\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{test}). Grouping
172	by span name tells you how many LLM calls occurred, not which categories
173	of work consumed the budget. Third, these limitations compound in practice: a common system effect
174	like running a test suite may appear thousands of times across sessions,

\subsection{How Existing Agent Trace Models Work}

Current agent observability tools organize traces around fixed
hierarchies. OpenTelemetry represents an execution as a \emph{trace}
containing a tree of \emph{spans}, each with a name, duration, and
key-value attributes. LangSmith and Langfuse group spans into
\emph{sessions} and display them as timelines or waterfall charts.
Phoenix and OpenInference add GenAI-specific span types for LLM calls,
tool invocations, retrieval steps, and agent reasoning.

These models share a structural property: the session or span tree is the
skeleton of the data. Every event belongs to exactly one span, and spans
nest in a fixed parent-child hierarchy determined at execution time.
This design is effective for debugging: a developer can locate a failing
span, inspect its attributes, and trace its parent chain to understand
the execution context.

\subsection{Why Fixed Hierarchies Cannot Profile}

Profiling requires a fundamentally different operation: \emph{folding}
events across executions by semantic category so that width represents
aggregate cost. Fixed session/span hierarchies obstruct this in three
ways.

First, sessions are boundaries, not categories: a single session may
contain review, debugging, and refactoring phases, and splitting by
session assigns all of them to the same bucket. Conversely, two sessions
performing the same task produce separate buckets that cannot be merged
without external logic. Second, span names describe mechanisms
(\texttt{LLMCall}, \texttt{ToolInvoke}, \texttt{ChatCompletion}), not
user intent (\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{test}). Grouping
by span name tells you how many LLM calls occurred, not which categories
of work consumed the budget. Third, these limitations compound in practice: a common system effect
like running a test suite may appear thousands of times across sessions,
but a flat process summary shows only a single counter with no way to
attribute executions to the semantic intent that triggered them. We
quantify this disaggregation in RQ1~(\S\ref{sec:eval}).

\subsection{Why CPU Profiling Does Not Directly Apply}

CPU profilers solve the equivalent aggregation problem for programs.
A flame graph~\cite{flamegraphs} represents a profile as a set of
weighted \emph{samples}, each attached to a \emph{call stack} (an
ordered list of function frames). Identical stacks merge, and width
represents aggregate cost. The key enabler is that function names are
\emph{deterministic}: the same code path always produces the same
frames.

Agent traces break this precondition. Prompts are natural language and
lack deterministic identifiers. Tool calls, GUI
actions, and process events are named heterogeneously across agent
families. Raw event names cannot serve as flame-graph frames.

These observations yield three design requirements:

\begin{description}
\item[R1: Uniform record type.]
  Agent traces mix prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions,
  process events, and benchmark labels. The profiler needs a single
  record type that can represent all of them without type-specific
  objects.
\item[R2: Query-time aggregation.]
  The same data must support multiple aggregation shapes---by task,
  phase, action, session, or dataset---without rebuilding the trace.
  Sessions and spans must be fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
\item[R3: Deterministic labels for folding.]
  Free-form prompts must be mapped to short, stable, repeatable labels
  before folding. This \emph{intent recognition} step has no analogue in
  CPU profiling, where function names are already deterministic.
\end{description}

\subsection{RQ1: Does Semantic Profiling Separate What Flat Views Mix?}

The strongest argument against semantic profiling is that traditional
tools ``can already see the same information.'' RQ1 tests this claim
directly by measuring how much system-effect weight falls into
\emph{mixed-intent} buckets---buckets containing observations from
multiple semantic regions---under different projection choices.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Semantic-axis ablation on 183{,}714 system observations
from 325 real sessions. All rows preserve the same total weight.}
\label{tab:mixing}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
Projection & Unique stacks & Mixed wt.\% & Residual\% \\
\midrule
No semantic labels & 11{,}967 & 90.4 & 44.7 \\
Session label only & 15{,}027 & 84.4 & 33.4 \\
Prompt label only & 24{,}703 & 36.7 & 7.5 \\
Session + prompt & 26{,}829 & 0.0 & 0.0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

prompts. Adding only the prompt label reduces mixed weight to 36.7\% and
residual to 7.5\%. The session label alone barely helps (84.4\%), because
sessions typically contain multiple intent phases.

A concrete example: \texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok}

## Round 7 — Flow and Polish Findings

### Must-fix

**FL-1: L22–44 — Abstract old-to-new thread breaks between beats 2→3.**
Beat 2 ends on "semantic work category." Beat 3 jumps to "We show that agent profiling reduces to two abstractions once intent recognition restores the deterministic-label precondition that flame-graph folding requires." The term "deterministic-label precondition" appears for the first time, requiring forward knowledge the reader does not yet have. The abstract should thread from the *gap* (can't fold) to the *solution* (two abstractions that restore foldability).

Fix: Replace the opening of beat 3 with something that builds on the gap. `"We show that two abstractions restore the ability to fold agent traces once a missing precondition---deterministic labels---is recovered through intent recognition."` (Moves the known gap to topic position, places the new abstractions in stress position.)

**FL-2: L92–97 — Intro ¶5 (key insight) stress position wasted on "remove this obstacle."**
The paragraph's most important new claim is *semantic profiling*, but the last sentence ends on "remove this obstacle," which is backward-pointing. The stress position should carry the forward-looking payoff.

Fix: Reorder the final sentence. `"The obstacle is the nondeterminism of natural-language identifiers. Intent recognition can restore deterministic labels, making semantic profiling tractable."` (Stress position now lands on "tractable" / the payoff, not the obstacle.)

**FL-3: L324 — Grammar error: "iterate" should be "iterates."**
"The developer runs…, observes…, adds…, re-runs, and iterate until unmatched drops below 5%." Subject is "The developer" (singular).

Fix: `"iterates"`

---

### Should-fix

**FL-4: L54–60 — Intro ¶1 stress position wasted on "families."**
The paragraph's topic is *heterogeneous traces at scale* and the new claim is *aggregate questions*. But the sentence ends on "semantic task families," which is a detail inside the list. The stress position should carry the main consequence.

Fix: Restructure the last clause. `"As deployments scale to hundreds of sessions and tens of thousands of calls, developers and automated analysis agents need aggregate views of which categories of work consume the most tokens, where failures concentrate, and how cost distributes."` (Drops "semantic task families" which is introduced properly later; stress lands on the aggregate-view concept.)

**FL-5: L63–70 — Intro ¶2 transition word "However" is adequate but the topic sentence buries the pain.**
"However, existing observability tools (…) organize events into per-execution timelines and span trees, enabling single-run debugging but not cross-session aggregation." The topic sentence names the tools before naming the problem. For a *problem* paragraph, lead with the gap.

Fix: `"However, no existing observability tool folds events across sessions into an aggregate cost distribution. LangSmith~\\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\\cite{langfuse}, Phoenix~\\cite{phoenix}, and OpenTelemetry GenAI~\\cite{otel} organize events into per-execution timelines and span trees, enabling single-run debugging but not cross-session aggregation."` (Gap in topic position, tools in supporting detail.)

**FL-6: L100–111 — Intro ¶6 repeats "restores" twice in 8 lines.**
L100: "restores aggregate flame-graph analysis." L104: "restores the deterministic-label precondition." Both sentences use "restores" as their main verb, creating lexical monotony in the most important system-description paragraph.

Fix: Change L104. `"\\toolname recovers the deterministic-label precondition through \\emph{intent recognition}, which maps free-form prompts to stable labels..."` (Alternates verb.)

**FL-7: L151–156 — Background §2.1 ¶2 three short sentences in sequence.**
"These models share a structural property. The session or span tree is the skeleton of the data. Every event belongs to exactly one span, and spans nest in a fixed parent-child hierarchy determined at execution time." Three sentences of 7, 12, and 18 words. The first two are note-like.

Fix: Merge the first two. `"These models share a structural property: the session or span tree is the skeleton of the data."` Wait — colons are restricted. Instead: `"These models share a structural property, namely that the session or span tree is the skeleton of the data."` (Merges the declaration and its content into one flowing sentence.)

**FL-8: L173 — Background §2.2 "Third" sentence is 45 words with no internal connector.**
"Third, these limitations compound in practice. A common system effect like running a test suite may appear thousands of times across sessions, but a flat process summary shows only a single counter with no way to attribute executions to the semantic intent that triggered them." The second sentence is 38 words. It flows adequately but could thread better by naming the consequence before the mechanism.

Fix: `"Third, these limitations compound in practice. A common system effect such as running a test suite may appear thousands of times across sessions, yet a flat process summary shows only a single counter and cannot attribute executions to the semantic intent behind them."` (Minor: "no way to attribute" → "cannot attribute" is more direct; "that triggered them" → "behind them" avoids the relative clause.)

**FL-9: L225–228 — Design §3.1 opening has a colon after "abstraction" introducing a definition.**
"\\toolname uses a single abstraction: an \\operation is a weighted record with string fields and additive measures." This is the last colon-before-definition remaining.

Fix: `"\\toolname uses a single abstraction. An \\operation is a weighted record with string fields and additive measures."`

**FL-10: L268–270 — Two short sentences then a trailing colon-like "questions:"**
"The view formalism supports arbitrary user-defined views. Four built-in defaults (Table~\\ref{tab:views}) answer common questions:" — this ends with a bare colon before the table, which is an unlabeled-list colon.

Fix: Remove the colon. `"Four built-in defaults (Table~\\ref{tab:views}) answer common questions."` (The table follows immediately; the colon adds nothing.)

**FL-11: L489–499 — RQ1 case-study paragraph has weak old-to-new threading.**
The paragraph starts with "These quantitative results translate to concrete aggregate insights." Then it jumps between tokens view, files view, network view, and files view again. Each sentence introduces a new view with no backward link. The paragraph reads as a list of examples rather than a building argument.

Fix: Add light threading between sentences. For example after the tokens-view sentence, link to files: `"The \\texttt{files} view reveals a complementary pattern: \\texttt{debug}-tagged prompts across different sessions repeatedly access the same source files..."` And after that, link the remaining views as a group: `"Similarly, the \\texttt{network} view attributes domain contacts to prompt categories, and the \\texttt{files} view identifies accesses outside the project root, supporting security auditing."`

**FL-12: L567–568 — Colon after a cross-reference.**
"The comparison also serves as evidence for the two-abstraction model (\\S\\ref{sec:design}): fixed-session drilldown and dataset-native hierarchy are alternative abstractions..." Last remaining colon in RQ2 body text.

Fix: Period. `"...model (\\S\\ref{sec:design}). Fixed-session drilldown and dataset-native hierarchy are alternative abstractions..."`

**FL-13: L704 — Related Work ¶1 uses a colon in "The difference is the domain:".**
"The difference is the domain: samples are agent operations, frames are semantic labels..."

Fix: Period. `"The difference is the domain. Samples are agent operations, frames are semantic labels..."`

**FL-14: L728–731 — Related Work ¶3 uses two colons in consecutive sentences.**
"...which step failed and why. \\toolname performs \\emph{category-level} aggregate profiling: which categories of work produce the most failures, consume the most budget, or generate repeated system effects across sessions." This is a colon-before-unlabeled-list.

Fix: Restructure. `"\\toolname performs \\emph{category-level} aggregate profiling, identifying which categories of work produce the most failures, consume the most budget, or generate repeated system effects across sessions."`

### Consider

**FL-15: L300 — Figure caption uses a semicolon.**
"Local agent histories enter through \\texttt{agent-session} parsing; public datasets enter as operation JSONL." — a semicolon joining independent clauses in a caption.

Fix: Period. `"...\\texttt{agent-session} parsing. Public datasets enter as operation JSONL."`

**FL-16: L683 — Terminology: "tags" vs "labels" drift reappears.**
"A display-governance pipeline reduces unique tags from 1,546 to 1,364 through deterministic aliases, raising top-20 support coverage from 93.7% to 95.2% without overwriting raw tags." — uses "tags" three times in one sentence where the rest of the paper now uses "labels."

The abstract's final sentence is "Leave-dataset-out mapping achieves V-measure above 0.7 on 7/9 held-out datasets." The stress position ("held-out datasets") is a methodological detail, not the payoff. The emphatic information is the V-measure score.

"The evaluation confirms that semantic profiling separates information flat views merge" — grammatically correct but garden-path. Readers parse "separates information" as a complete clause, then must re-parse "flat views merge" as a relative clause.

The abstract should thread from the *gap* (can't fold) to the *solution* (two abstractions that restore foldability).

Fix: Replace the opening of beat 3 with something that builds on the gap. `"We show that two abstractions restore the ability to fold agent traces once a missing precondition---deterministic labels---is recovered through intent recognition."` (Moves the known gap to topic position, places the new abstractions in stress position.)

**FL-2: L92–97 — Intro ¶5 (key insight) stress position wasted on "remove this obstacle."**

"The developer runs…, observes…, adds…, re-runs, and iterate until unmatched drops below 5%." Subject is "The developer" (singular).

**FL-4: L54–60 — Intro ¶1 stress position wasted on "families."**
The paragraph's topic is *heterogeneous traces at scale* and the new claim is *aggregate questions*. But the sentence ends on "semantic task families," which is a detail inside the list. The stress position should carry the main consequence.

Fix: Restructure the last clause. `"As deployments scale to hundreds of sessions and tens of thousands of calls, developers and automated analysis agents need aggregate views of which categories of work consume the most tokens, where failures concentrate, and how cost distributes."` (Drops "semantic task families" which is introduced properly later; stress lands on the aggregate-view concept.)

**FL-5: L63–70 — Intro ¶2 transition word "However" is adequate but the topic sentence buries the pain.**
"However, existing observability tools (…) organize events into per-execution timelines and span trees, enabling single-run debugging but not cross-session aggregation." The topic sentence names the tools before naming the problem. For a *problem* paragraph, lead with the gap.

**FL-6: L100–111 — Intro ¶6 repeats "restores" twice in 8 lines.**

"Third, these limitations compound in practice. content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /home/yunwei37/.claude/skills/check-paper-citations

# Citation Verification

Systematically verify every citation in a paper. This skill reads cited papers, confirms they exist, checks that claims match sources, and maintains a structured annotation system in the .bib file.

## First Step

Read the paper's `.tex` file and `.bib` file. Identify the `docs/reference/` directory (or create it) for storing downloaded PDFs.

Then run the three passes below in order. Do not skip passes.

## Pass 1: Existence and Authenticity

For every entry in the `.bib` file:

1. **Check the bib annotation block.** Look for a comment block above each entry with these fields:
   ```bibtex
   % VERIFIED: <date>
   % REAL: yes|no|unverified
   % PDF: <path or "not available">
   % ABSTRACT: <1-2 sentence summary of what the paper actually says>
   % USED_FOR: <what this paper uses it for, in our context>
   ```
   If this block is missing or incomplete, the entry needs full verification.

2. **Verify the paper exists.** For each unverified entry:
   - Search for the paper by title on the web (arxiv, ACM DL, IEEE, USENIX, Google Scholar)
   - Confirm: title matches, authors match, year matches, venue matches
   - If the paper does not exist or metadata is wrong, flag as **HALLUCINATED** (must-fix)
   - If found, download the PDF to `docs/reference/<citekey>.pdf`

3. **Read the abstract and introduction** of each downloaded PDF. Write a 1-2 sentence summary of what the paper actually says (its main contribution, not what we want it to say).

4. **Update the .bib annotation block** with all fields filled in.

## Pass 2: Claim-Citation Alignment

For every `\cite{}` in the `.tex` file:

1. **Extract the surrounding claim.** Read the sentence containing the citation and 1-2 surrounding sentences for context.

2. **Check: does the cited paper support this claim?**
   - Read the cited paper's abstract/intro (from PDF or annotation)
   - Does the paper actually say what we claim it says?
   - Common problems:
     - Mischaracterization: "Paper X shows Y" but Paper X actually shows Z
     - Over-attribution: claiming the paper says more than it does
     - Context mismatch: using a finding from one context to support a claim in a different context

3. **If a claim is inaccurate:**
   - Report as Must-fix with: the claim text, what the paper actually says, and a suggested rewrite
   - Edit the `.tex` to fix the claim (with Chinese translation if the paper uses bilingual format)
   - Update the `USED_FOR` field in the .bib annotation

## Pass 3: Missing Citations

Scan the paper for claims that need citations but don't have them:

1. **Factual claims without support.** Statements like "X% of Y" or "research shows that Z" without a citation.

2. **System comparisons.** Mentions of other systems (Docker, gVisor, Firecracker, etc.) that should cite the original paper.

3. **Technique attributions.** "The dual-LLM pattern" or "the lethal trifecta" — are the original sources cited?

4. **Background knowledge.** Claims about kernel mechanisms (Landlock, seccomp) that cite documentation or papers.

For each missing citation:
- Report as Should-fix
- Suggest which paper to cite (search if needed)
- Add the bib entry with full annotations if a citation is added

## Bib Annotation Format

Every bib entry must have this comment block immediately above it:

```bibtex
% VERIFIED: 2026-07-07
% REAL: yes
% PDF: docs/reference/agentcgroup.pdf
% ABSTRACT: Characterizes OS-level resource dynamics of AI coding agents
%   across 144 tasks. Finds container-level resource controls are
%   mismatched with tool-call-level dynamics (granularity, responsiveness,
%   adaptability mismatches).
% USED_FOR: Motivation for per-tool-call granularity (resource dimension)
@misc{agentcgroup,
  title={...},
  ...
}
```

Fields:
- `VERIFIED`: Date of last verification (YYYY-MM-DD)
- `REAL`: `yes` (confirmed real), `no` (hallucinated, must remove), `unverified`
- `PDF`: Path to downloaded PDF, or "not available" if not downloadable
- `ABSTRACT`: Factual summary of what the paper says (2-3 lines max)
- `USED_FOR`: How our paper uses this citation (1 line)

## Output

After all three passes, report:
- Number of citations verified
- Number of hallucinated citations (must-fix)
- Number of inaccurate claims fixed
- Number of missing citations added
- Any entries that could not be verified (PDF not available, etc.)

## When Called from iter-refine-writing

When triggered as a gate check (not a full run):
- Only check whether all .bib entries have complete annotation blocks
- If any annotation is missing or has `REAL: unverified`, trigger a full run of this skill
- If all annotations are present and `REAL: yes`, just check for missing citations in the .tex (Pass 3 only)

Based on the search results, I found the ArXiv paper you're looking for:

AgentAtlas is intended to help benchmark designers state what behavior they cover, and to help evaluators diagnose failures that outcome-only leaderboards hide. AgentAtlas reframes agent evaluation as a diagnostic vocabulary and audit protocol for separating outcome success from control-decision quality and trajectory quality.

The paper's key contributions include: a six-state control-decision taxonomy (Act / Ask / Refuse / Stop / Confirm / Recover); a trajectory-failure vocabulary with primary error source and downstream impact; a 0/1/2 benchmark-coverage audit over fifteen agent benchmarks; and an illustrative protocol study on a synthetic 1,342-item set evaluated with eight models under taxonomy-aware and taxonomy-blind prompt formats.

The paper was published on ArXiv in May 2026 (arXiv ID: 2605.20530) and addresses the fragmentation of agent evaluation benchmarks by providing a more nuanced framework for assessing LLM agent behavior beyond just final task success.

## Overview

ScaleCUA is a step toward scaling open-source computer use agents (CUAs), offering a large-scale dataset spanning 6 operating systems and 3 task domains, built via a closed-loop pipeline uniting automated agents with human experts.

## Background

Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have enabled computer use agents (CUAs) that operate GUIs autonomously, showing great potential, yet progress is limited by the lack of large-scale, open-source computer use data and foundation models.

## Key Approach

Based on the search results, here's what I found about tau-bench:

## τ-bench Benchmark Overview

τ-bench is a benchmark that emulates dynamic conversations between a user (simulated by language models) and a language agent provided with domain-specific API tools and policy guidelines. The benchmark was designed to evaluate language agents on realistic, multi-turn customer service tasks, simulating interactions within two retail domains: an airline reservation system and a retail e-commerce platform.

## Retail and Airline Domains

In the airline domain (τ-airline), tasks involve flight bookings, cancellations, seat upgrades, loyalty program queries, and itinerary modifications, with a database including flight schedules, fare classes, passenger records, and loyalty account details. In the retail domain (τ-retail), tasks involve order management, returns, exchanges, product inquiries, and account modifications, with a database including product catalogs, order histories, inventory, and customer profiles.

## Evaluation and Performance

The benchmark proposes a new metric (pass^k) to evaluate the reliability of agent behavior over multiple trials. Experiments show that even state-of-the-art function calling agents (like gpt-4o) succeed on less than 50% of the tasks, and are quite inconsistent (pass^8 <25% in retail).

## Recent Updates (2025)

τ-bench is a recently introduced benchmark to measure the reliability of language agents in multi-turn task-oriented conversations such as customer service workflows, while respecting domain rules. Additionally, a recent version included 75+ task quality fixes, removing incorrect expected actions, clarifying ambiguous instructions, fixing impossible constraints, and adding missing fallback behaviors across airline, retail, and banking domains.

Based on the search results, I found information about AgentTrek:

AgentTrek is a method for generating trajectories for Graphical User Interface (GUI) agents to automate complex tasks across digital environments. AgentTrek is a scalable data synthesis pipeline that generates web agent trajectories by leveraging publicly available tutorials.

The three-stage method automatically harvests and filters tutorial-like texts from the internet using a specialized classification model, transforms these texts into structured task specifications with step-by-step instructions, and employs a visual-language model (VLM) agent to execute these instructions in real environments, while a VLM-based evaluator verifies trajectory correctness.

The paper was submitted to arXiv on December 12, 2024, with the identifier arXiv:2412.09605. The authors are Yiheng Xu, Dunjie Lu, Zhennan Shen, Junli Wang, Zekun Wang, Yuchen Mao, Caiming Xiong, and Tao Yu.

Based on the search results, I found comprehensive information about the GUI-Odyssey benchmark:

## GUI-Odyssey: Cross-App GUI Navigation Benchmark

GUI Odyssey is the first large-scale cross-application GUI navigation dataset—comprising 7,735 multi-device navigation trajectories across 201 applications and 1,400 application combinations.

### Paper Details

The paper was authored by Q. Lu, W. Shao, Z. Liu, F. Meng, B. Li, B. Chen, S. Huang, K. Zhang, Y. Qiao, and P. Luo in 2024, and published on arXiv as arXiv preprint arXiv:2406.08451.

### Purpose and Scope

Prior GUI agents often trained with datasets comprising simple tasks that can be completed within a single app, leading to poor performance in cross-app navigation. To address this problem, GUI Odyssey is a comprehensive dataset for training and evaluating cross-app navigation agents.

### OdysseyAgent Performance

The authors developed OdysseyAgent as part of this work. OdysseyAgent is a multimodal cross-app navigation agent by fine-tuning the Qwen-VL model with a history resampling module. OdysseyAgent surpasses fine-tuned Qwen-VL and zero-shot GPT-4V by 1.44% and 55.49% in-domain accuracy, and 2.29% and 48.14% out-of-domain accuracy on average.

### Latest Version

The GUIOdyssey paper was accepted to ICCV 2025, and the dataset continues to be maintained and updated on GitHub.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /home/yunwei37/.claude/skills/check-paper-citations

# Citation Verification

Systematically verify every citation in a paper. This skill reads cited papers, confirms they exist, checks that claims match sources, and maintains a structured annotation system in the .bib file.

## First Step

Read the paper's `.tex` file and `.bib` file. Identify the `docs/reference/` directory (or create it) for storing downloaded PDFs.

**All citations must live in a standalone `.bib` file** (e.g., `references.bib`), never as inline `\bibitem{}` in the `.tex` file. If the paper uses `\bibitem{}`, migrate all entries to a `.bib` file first and switch to `\bibliography{references}`.

Then run the three passes below in order. Do not skip passes.

## Pass 1: Existence and Authenticity

For every entry in the `.bib` file:

1. **Check the bib annotation block.** Look for a comment block above each entry with these fields:
   ```bibtex
   % VERIFIED: <date>
   % REAL: yes|no|unverified
   % PDF: <path or "not available">
   % ABSTRACT: <1-2 sentence summary of what the paper actually says>
   % USED_FOR: <what this paper uses it for, in our context>
   ```
   If this block is missing or incomplete, the entry needs full verification.

2. **Verify the paper exists and metadata is correct.** For each unverified entry:
   - Search for the paper by title on the web (arxiv, ACM DL, IEEE, USENIX, Google Scholar)
   - Confirm ALL metadata fields: title, authors (full list, correct spelling), year, venue/booktitle, pages, DOI
   - If any metadata is wrong, fix it in the .bib entry
   - If the paper does not exist at all, flag as **HALLUCINATED** (must-fix)
   - If found, download the PDF to `docs/reference/<citekey>.pdf`
   - **Do NOT remove unused bib entries.** Mark them with `% STATUS: unused` but keep them. Only flag hallucinated entries for removal. The author may intend to use them later.

3. **Read the abstract and introduction** of each downloaded PDF. Write a 1-2 sentence summary of what the paper actually says (its main contribution, not what we want it to say).

4. **Update the .bib annotation block** with all fields filled in.

## Pass 2: Claim-Citation Alignment

For every `\cite{}` in the `.tex` file:

1. **Extract the surrounding claim.** Read the sentence containing the citation and 1-2 surrounding sentences for context.

2. **Check: does the cited paper support this claim?**
   - Read the cited paper's abstract/intro (from PDF or annotation)
   - Does the paper actually say what we claim it says?
   - Common problems:
     - Mischaracterization: "Paper X shows Y" but Paper X actually shows Z
     - Over-attribution: claiming the paper says more than it does
     - Context mismatch: using a finding from one context to support a claim in a different context

3. **If a claim is inaccurate:**
   - Report as Must-fix with: the claim text, what the paper actually says, and a suggested rewrite
   - Edit the `.tex` to fix the claim (with Chinese translation if the paper uses bilingual format)
   - Update the `USED_FOR` field in the .bib annotation

## Pass 3: Missing Citations

Scan the paper for claims that need citations but don't have them:

1. **Factual claims without support.** Statements like "X% of Y" or "research shows that Z" without a citation.

2. **System comparisons.** Mentions of other systems (Docker, gVisor, Firecracker, etc.) that should cite the original paper.

3. **Technique attributions.** "The dual-LLM pattern" or "the lethal trifecta" — are the original sources cited?

4. **Background knowledge.** Claims about kernel mechanisms (Landlock, seccomp) that cite documentation or papers.

For each missing citation:
- Report as Should-fix
- Suggest which paper to cite (search if needed)
- Add the bib entry with full annotations if a citation is added

## Bib Annotation Format

Every bib entry must have this comment block immediately above it:

```bibtex
% VERIFIED: 2026-07-07
% REAL: yes
% PDF: docs/reference/agentcgroup.pdf
% ABSTRACT: Characterizes OS-level resource dynamics of AI coding agents
%   across 144 tasks. Finds container-level resource controls are
%   mismatched with tool-call-level dynamics (granularity, responsiveness,
%   adaptability mismatches).
% USED_FOR: Motivation for per-tool-call granularity (resource dimension)
@misc{agentcgroup,
  title={...},
  ...
}
```

Fields:
- `VERIFIED`: Date of last verification (YYYY-MM-DD)
- `REAL`: `yes` (confirmed real), `no` (hallucinated, must remove), `unverified`
- `PDF`: Path to downloaded PDF, or "not available" if not downloadable
- `ABSTRACT`: Factual summary of what the paper says (2-3 lines max)
- `USED_FOR`: How our paper uses this citation (1 line)

## Verification Ledger

Maintain a standalone file `docs/citation-verification.md` alongside the bib annotations. This file records the verification state of every citation in one place:

```markdown
# Citation Verification Ledger

Last full run: 2026-07-07

| citekey | REAL | Authors verified | Metadata correct | PDF | Claim accurate | Notes |
|---------|------|-----------------|------------------|-----|----------------|-------|
| camel | yes | yes | yes | docs/reference/camel.pdf | fixed L142 | CaMeL is enforcement, not "assumes" it |
| agentcgroup | yes | yes | yes | docs/reference/agentcgroup.pdf | fixed L140 | removed wrong attribution |
| kgent | yes | yes | yes | not downloaded | unused | keep for potential reference |
```

Update this file after every run. The bib annotations are the authoritative source; the ledger is a summary for quick review.

## Output

After all three passes, report:
- Number of citations verified
- Number of hallucinated citations (must-fix)
- Number of inaccurate claims fixed
- Number of missing citations added
- Any entries that could not be verified (PDF not available, etc.)

## When Called from iter-refine-writing

When triggered as a gate check (not a full run):
- Only check whether all .bib entries have complete annotation blocks
- If any annotation is missing or has `REAL: unverified`, trigger a full run of this skill
- If all annotations are present and `REAL: yes`, just check for missing citations in the .tex (Pass 3 only)

Base directory for this skill: /home/yunwei37/.claude/skills/check-paper-citations

# Citation Verification

Systematically verify every citation in a paper. This skill reads cited papers, confirms they exist, checks that claims match sources, and maintains a structured annotation system in the .bib file.

## First Step

Read the paper's `.tex` file and `.bib` file. Identify the `docs/reference/` directory (or create it) for storing downloaded PDFs.

**All citations must live in a standalone `.bib` file** (e.g., `references.bib`), never as inline `\bibitem{}` in the `.tex` file. If the paper uses `\bibitem{}`, migrate all entries to a `.bib` file first and switch to `\bibliography{references}`.

Then run the three passes below in order. Do not skip passes.

## Pass 1: Existence and Authenticity

For every entry in the `.bib` file:

1. **Check the bib annotation block.** Look for a comment block above each entry with these fields:
   ```bibtex
   % VERIFIED: <date>
   % REAL: yes|no|unverified
   % PDF: <path or "not available">
   % ABSTRACT: <1-2 sentence summary of what the paper actually says>
   % USED_FOR: <what this paper uses it for, in our context>
   ```
   If this block is missing or incomplete, the entry needs full verification.

2. **Verify the paper exists and metadata is correct.** For each unverified entry:
   - Search for the paper by title on the web (arxiv, ACM DL, IEEE, USENIX, Google Scholar)
   - Confirm ALL metadata fields: title, authors (full list, correct spelling), year, venue/booktitle, pages, DOI
   - If any metadata is wrong, fix it in the .bib entry
   - If the paper does not exist at all, flag as **HALLUCINATED** (must-fix)
   - If found, download the PDF to `docs/reference/<citekey>.pdf`
   - **Do NOT remove unused bib entries.** Mark them with `% STATUS: unused` but keep them. Only flag hallucinated entries for removal. The author may intend to use them later.

3. **Read the abstract and introduction** of each downloaded PDF. Write a 1-2 sentence summary of what the paper actually says (its main contribution, not what we want it to say).

4. **Update the .bib annotation block** with all fields filled in.

## Pass 2: Claim-Citation Alignment

For every `\cite{}` in the `.tex` file:

1. **Extract the surrounding claim.** Read the sentence containing the citation and 1-2 surrounding sentences for context.

2. **Check: does the cited paper support this claim?**
   - Read the cited paper's abstract/intro (from PDF or annotation)
   - Does the paper actually say what we claim it says?
   - Common problems:
     - Mischaracterization: "Paper X shows Y" but Paper X actually shows Z
     - Over-attribution: claiming the paper says more than it does
     - Context mismatch: using a finding from one context to support a claim in a different context

3. **If a claim is inaccurate:**
   - Report as Must-fix with: the claim text, what the paper actually says, and a suggested rewrite
   - Edit the `.tex` to fix the claim (with Chinese translation if the paper uses bilingual format)
   - Update the `USED_FOR` field in the .bib annotation

## Pass 2.5: Academic Integrity Checks

For every citation, check for these additional risks:

1. **Preprint vs published version.** If a bib entry cites an arXiv preprint, check whether a published (conference/journal) version now exists. If yes, update the bib entry to cite the published version with correct venue, pages, and DOI.

2. **Secondary citations.** If the paper attributes a claim to source A, but source A itself attributes it to source B, the paper should cite B directly (or cite both). Check key claims against their cited sources.

3. **String citations in claims.** `\cite{a,b,c}` chains are fine in related work surveys. Only flag when a specific factual claim in the paper's own argument rests on a chain without explaining which source supports it.

4. **Self-citation and double-blind.** Self-citation is encouraged — it shows research continuity. But under double-blind review:
   - Self-citations must use third person ("X et al." not "our prior work")
   - Flag if the .tex text says "our" or "we" when referring to a cited paper that shares authors
   - Do NOT flag self-citations as a problem — flag only identity leaks

5. **Retracted papers.** For each academic paper citation, check if it has been retracted (search for retraction notices).

6. **Venue accuracy.** Confirm that the venue/booktitle in the bib matches where the paper was actually published. Common errors: citing a workshop paper as a main conference paper, or vice versa.

7. **Ghost citations.** If a bib entry is cited (`\cite{X}` appears) but the surrounding text never explains WHY it is cited, flag as Should-fix. Every citation should earn its place.

## Pass 3: Missing Citations

Scan the paper for citation gaps. This pass both checks existing text AND actively searches for missing citations.

### 3a. Factual claims without support
Statements like "X% of Y", "research shows that Z", or "agents invoke dozens of calls per minute" without a citation. Every factual claim that is not the paper's own measurement or common knowledge needs a cite.

### 3b. System and technique mentions
Every named system (Docker, gVisor, Firecracker, etc.) and technique (dual-LLM, lethal trifecta, least privilege) should cite the original source at first mention.

### 3c. Citation density by section
Check citation density per section. Flag sections where the ratio of claims to citations is low:
- **Introduction** — should have a cite every 2-3 sentences on average
- **Background/Motivation** — should be the MOST densely cited section. Nearly every factual sentence needs a cite. Flag if any paragraph has fewer than 1 cite per 2 sentences.
- **Design** — lower density OK (it's the paper's own contribution), but borrowed concepts still need cites
- **Related Work** — every paragraph should cite multiple papers

### 3d. Actively search and add missing citations
For each gap found, do not just flag — **actively search** for the right paper to cite:
- Use WebSearch / WebFetch to find papers
- Download the PDF to `docs/reference/`
- Add the bib entry with full annotation block (VERIFIED, REAL, PDF, ABSTRACT, USED_FOR)
- Edit the .tex to add the `\cite{}` at the right location (with Chinese translation if the paper uses bilingual format)

Common citations that background sections often need:
- Classic principles: least privilege (Saltzer & Schroeder 1975), capability-based security (Dennis & Van Horn 1966)
- Agent frameworks: Claude Code, OpenHands, SWE-Agent, Devin — cite the relevant ones
- Measurement claims: if you say "dozens of calls per minute", cite AgentCgroup or your own measurement
- Kernel mechanisms: cite original papers or documentation for Landlock, seccomp, namespaces, cgroups

**Note:** For a comprehensive related-work coverage audit (are there important papers in the field that the paper doesn't discuss at all?), use `research-literature-novelty` separately. This pass focuses on citation gaps in the existing text.

## Bib Annotation Format

Every bib entry must have this comment block immediately above it:

```bibtex
% VERIFIED: 2026-07-07
% REAL: yes
% PDF: docs/reference/agentcgroup.pdf
% ABSTRACT: Characterizes OS-level resource dynamics of AI coding agents
%   across 144 tasks. Finds container-level resource controls are
%   mismatched with tool-call-level dynamics (granularity, responsiveness,
%   adaptability mismatches).
% USED_FOR: Motivation for per-tool-call granularity (resource dimension)
@misc{agentcgroup,
  title={...},
  ...
}
```

Fields:
- `VERIFIED`: Date of last verification (YYYY-MM-DD)
- `REAL`: `yes` (confirmed real), `no` (hallucinated, must remove), `unverified`
- `PDF`: Path to downloaded PDF, or "not available" if not downloadable
- `ABSTRACT`: Factual summary of what the paper says (2-3 lines max)
- `USED_FOR`: How our paper uses this citation (1 line)

## Verification Ledger

Maintain a standalone file `docs/citation-verification.md` alongside the bib annotations. This file records the verification state of every citation in one place:

```markdown
# Citation Verification Ledger

Last full run: 2026-07-07

| citekey | REAL | Authors verified | Metadata correct | PDF | Claim accurate | Notes |
|---------|------|-----------------|------------------|-----|----------------|-------|
| camel | yes | yes | yes | docs/reference/camel.pdf | fixed L142 | CaMeL is enforcement, not "assumes" it |
| agentcgroup | yes | yes | yes | docs/reference/agentcgroup.pdf | fixed L140 | removed wrong attribution |
| kgent | yes | yes | yes | not downloaded | unused | keep for potential reference |
```

Update this file after every run. The bib annotations are the authoritative source; the ledger is a summary for quick review.

## Output

After all three passes, report:
- Number of citations verified
- Number of hallucinated citations (must-fix)
- Number of inaccurate claims fixed
- Number of missing citations added
- Any entries that could not be verified (PDF not available, etc.)

## When Called from iter-refine-writing

When triggered as a gate check (not a full run):
- Only check whether all .bib entries have complete annotation blocks
- If any annotation is missing or has `REAL: unverified`, trigger a full run of this skill
- If all annotations are present and `REAL: yes`, just check for missing citations in the .tex (Pass 3 only)
